# Kingston Line

## Kingston Line (Jamaica)

The term "Kingston Line" refers to the historic railway infrastructure centered on Kingston, Jamaica, which served as the capital city's main transportation hub and the birthplace of the nation's entire rail network , . This line is defined operationally by the Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC) as the rail corridor connecting the towns of Spanish Town and Kingston . Its history is foundational to Jamaica's development, beginning as the island's inaugural railway and expanding into a comprehensive system that linked the capital to all fourteen of Jamaica's parishes , . The line's story encompasses pioneering engineering, significant urban development, a tragic national disaster, and a contemporary push for revival aimed at modernizing the country's transport infrastructure , . The physical remnants, most notably the derelict yet historically designated Kingston Railway Terminus, stand as a testament to its past prominence and a potential catalyst for future urban regeneration , .

The genesis of the Kingston Line occurred on November 21, 1845, when the Western Jamaica Connecting Railway opened a 19-kilometer (12-mile) single-track line running from Kingston to Spanish Town , , . This inaugural segment, measuring 14.5 miles (23.3 km), marked the first railway line opened to traffic outside of Europe and North America and the first constructed within the British colonies . The project, proposed by William and David Smith in 1843, was incorporated under the 7th Victoria Cap. 25 and inaugurated by Governor James Bruce, 8th Earl of Elgin, who used locomotives named Projector and Patriot, built by Sharp Brothers of Manchester , . This initial line established Kingston as the primary southern terminus of the nascent national railway system . Construction of the broader network began in phases, transforming the Kingston-Spanish Town line into the core of an extensive web of tracks. The expansion proceeded as follows: Phase one, completed in 1845, connected Kingston to Angels (just north of Spanish Town) over 14.5 miles; phase two, added in 1869, extended the line another 11 miles to Old Harbour; phase three, completed in 1885, pushed the track 24.5 miles further to Porus; and finally, phase four, completed in 1895, saw the line reach Montego Bay, adding a 62-mile stretch . This resulted in the Kingston to Montego Bay railway becoming Jamaica's main trunk line, operating from 1845 until 1992 and passing through most of the island's major towns . The entire system operated on a standard gauge of 4 feet 8+1⁄2 inches (1,435 mm) .

From its central hub in downtown Kingston, the railway network radiated outward via several key passenger lines, establishing the city as a vital transportation nexus . The primary routes originating from the Kingston Railway Terminus included the main line to Montego Bay, a branch line to Ewarton via Spanish Town, a branch to Port Antonio via Bog Walk, and a final branch to Frankfield via May Pen . By the mid-20th century, the system had grown to encompass 210 miles (340 km) of track, serving all 14 parishes of Jamaica and connecting the capital to the country's other major population centers and economic hubs . The government-owned railway, which came under the administration of the Jamaica Government Railway from 1900, played a crucial role in the island's economic life, facilitating the movement of people and goods across the island . Passenger service was a defining feature of the system, with notable amenities such as travelling post office (TPO) carriages being introduced in 1913, which remained in use until the last run on May 14, 1966 . The network's expansion and integration into the fabric of Jamaican life were reflected in the uniformity of its station architecture. Between 1845 and 1896, all 17 stations built along the various lines—including those in Kingston, Spanish Town, Appleton, Montego Bay, Linstead, and Bog Walk—were designed in a consistent Jamaica/Georgian architectural style . These structures, predominantly made of timber or brick, featured distinctive two-storey forms and have since become important examples of colonial-era industrial design, though many are now in disrepair or have been repurposed .

The heart of the Kingston Line was the Kingston Railway Terminus, a grand facility that served as the origin point for all four main passenger lines . Constructed in the Jamaica Georgian architectural style using brick with prominent arcades and Victorian cast iron brackets, the terminus was a complex piece of infrastructure . It featured a single platform, extensive sidings for storing rolling stock, engine sheds, repair works, a roundhouse, a turntable for reversing locomotives, and a traverser to move cars between tracks . A critical component of the terminus was its direct connection to railway piers, facilitating the transfer of cargo and passengers between ships and trains . The building itself, located in downtown Kingston, opened in 1845 and functioned as the bustling nerve center of Jamaica's rail operations for nearly 150 years until passenger service ceased permanently in October 1992 , . Despite its closure, the terminus remains a significant historical landmark. It has been listed as a designated National Heritage Site by the Jamaica National Heritage Trust, recognizing its architectural and historical value . While some sources describe it as "sadly derelict," indicating its current state of neglect, its preservation ensures its potential for future restoration . One source claims the terminus was 'utterly destroyed' in the 1907 Kingston earthquake, but a 2003 report from the Ministry of Transport and Works described it as being in "very good condition" and requiring only minor repairs, suggesting a discrepancy in accounts of its post-earthquake survival .

The decline and eventual cessation of the Kingston Line's passenger service in October 1992 was precipitated by a combination of factors, primarily a lack of government funding and declining passenger usage , . As road networks improved and automobile ownership became more widespread, the railways struggled to compete, leading to a steady erosion of ridership and revenue. This economic pressure, coupled with insufficient investment from successive governments, rendered the system financially unsustainable. Although passenger service ended abruptly, some freight operations continued, particularly those related to the bauxite industry, which utilized dedicated lines and infrastructure serving Kingston , . The broader context of this decline is tied to Jamaica's economic restructuring in the late 20th century. Successive IMF agreements, starting with the 1978 program, initiated decades of policy shifts that included privatization of state-owned enterprises and reductions in public spending . The Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC) itself has been slated for privatization as part of these structural adjustment programs, reflecting a broader trend of divesting state control over key economic sectors . This process has contributed to the abandonment of large sections of the railway network, with lines progressively decommissioned over the years .

In recent years, there has been a concerted effort to revive the Kingston Line and restore its role in Jamaica's transportation landscape. The Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC), a statutory body established under the Jamaica Railway Corporation Act of 1960, has outlined ambitious plans for revitalization , . A key initiative involves launching new passenger and freight train services between Spanish Town and Kingston . Preparations for this project are scheduled to commence during the Fiscal Year ending March 31, 2025 (FY 2024/25) , . The JRC's strategy includes concrete actions such as track reconstruction, the acquisition of new trains, the construction of necessary infrastructure, and discussions with private investors to secure funding for the rehabilitation project . This revitalization effort is supported by international partners, most notably the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB). In November 2024, the IDB approved a USD 175,000 technical cooperation grant for Jamaica's railways, a non-reimbursable grant classified as 'Sovereign Guaranteed' . This funding is explicitly intended to support railway infrastructure and aligns directly with the JRC's FY 2024/25 plans, providing crucial backing for the restoration of the Spanish Town–Kingston corridor . The vision for the revived Kingston Line extends beyond mere transportation; proponents see it as a catalyst for urban and economic development. The restoration of train service to the historic Kingston Railway Terminus is envisioned as a way to re-establish the city center as a vibrant transportation hub, drawing parallels to European models where railway stations serve as the heart of urban life . This initiative represents a significant attempt to reclaim a piece of national heritage and adapt it for the needs of a modern Jamaica.

A pivotal and tragic event in the history of the Jamaican railway system was the Kendal rail disaster of September 1, 1957 . At approximately 11:30 p.m., a train departing Kingston bound for Montego Bay crashed near the village of Kendal , . The disaster resulted in an estimated 200 fatalities and between 400 and 700 injuries, making it the worst transportation tragedy in Jamaica's history and, at the time, the second-worst rail disaster globally . The Kendal crash stands as a profound turning point, marking a moment of immense public trauma that likely accelerated the loss of confidence in the railway system and contributed significantly to the long-term decline in passenger usage that culminated in the full cessation of services in 1992 . The legacy of this event underscores the inherent risks of early railway operations and serves as a somber reminder of the human cost associated with the industrialization of transport. Today, the original Kingston-Spanish Town line, the very first segment of the Kingston Line, survives in a state of partial dereliction but continues to be a focus of preservation efforts. The Jamaica Community Rail Project (JCRP) is actively working to transform the abandoned station buildings and the surrounding rail line into a tourist attraction, preserving a tangible link to Jamaica's rich railway past . Stations along this historic route, such as Gregory Park and Grange Lane, and the terminus at Angels’ Halt, remain as silent witnesses to the era of steam and steel that once defined the island's connectivity .

## Kingston Line (Canada)

The term "Kingston Line" in a Canadian context refers to the Kingston Subdivision, a major and heavily trafficked railway corridor owned primarily by Canadian National Railway (CN) . This line is a critical artery of North American rail transport, serving as the principal high-speed route connecting Toronto's Union Station with Montreal Central Station , . Historically, it originated as the main trunk line of the Grand Trunk Railway in the 1850s, establishing the foundational rail link between Canada's two largest metropolitan areas . The Kingston Subdivision runs primarily along the north shore of Lake Ontario and the Saint Lawrence River, forming a continuous and vital link in the continent's freight and passenger network , . Unlike its Jamaican counterpart, which has experienced periods of decay and revival, the Kingston Subdivision is a modern, technologically advanced, and economically indispensable asset. Its operations are characterized by high volumes of both freight and passenger traffic, sophisticated centralized traffic control, and the ongoing challenges of managing safety within a high-intensity environment. The line's history is intertwined with the consolidation of Canadian railways, while its present-day narrative is defined by its role in moving essential goods and intercity travelers across one of the world's busiest corridors.

The Kingston Subdivision was originally constructed in the 1850s by the Grand Trunk Railway (GTR) as its main route between Toronto and Montreal . This choice of alignment proved prescient, as the line's proximity to the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway facilitated the seamless transfer of cargo between rail and marine vessels, cementing its importance in the national economy. Over time, the GTR was absorbed by the Canadian National Railway, which continues to own and operate the majority of the line today . The ownership structure of the subdivision is unique in that it is shared among different operators. CN owns and operates the section east of Pickering Junction, Ontario, all the way to Dorval East in Montréal , . However, the segment from Union Station Rail Corridor in Toronto to Pickering Junction is owned by Metrolinx, the regional transportation agency for the Greater Toronto Area . This portion is exclusively used by GO Transit for its Lakeshore East commuter rail service , . VIA Rail, Canada's national passenger train operator, utilizes the entire length of the Kingston Subdivision for its intercity services, operating trains on both the Toronto-Montreal and Toronto-Ottawa corridors , . This multi-operator model makes the Kingston Subdivision a prime example of a shared-use corridor, balancing the demands of heavy-duty freight, high-frequency commuter transit, and long-distance passenger travel.

Operationally, the Kingston Subdivision is a high-capacity, high-speed rail line engineered for maximum efficiency. It is a standard gauge line (1,435 mm), identical to its Jamaican counterpart, ensuring compatibility with other major North American rail systems , . The line consists of two to four main tracks, allowing for the simultaneous passage of trains traveling in opposite directions . Traffic management is handled by a sophisticated Centralized Traffic Control (CTC) system, which has been in place since 1995 , . This technology allows a single traffic controller, based remotely in Edmonton, Alberta, to manage train movements across vast distances, eliminating the need for traditional block signals and manual clearance forms (OCS) . This level of automation is essential for handling the line's substantial daily traffic load. On average, the Kingston Subdivision carries approximately 18 CN freight trains and 12 VIA passenger trains each day . Freight operations include everything from intermodal containers to bulk commodities, while passenger services range from the high-speed Toronto-Montreal runs to the slower Toronto-Ottawa trains that diverge from the main line at Brockville . The line's ability to accommodate speeds of up to 90 mph for VIA trains and 60-90 mph for other passenger services highlights its design for high-performance transit . The complexity of this mixed-use environment is managed through a network of over 50 interlocking crossover tracks, which allow for the efficient interchange of trains, particularly between CN's freight fleet and VIA's passenger fleet .

Despite its technological sophistication and economic importance, the Kingston Subdivision is not immune to operational challenges and safety concerns. The sheer density of traffic creates constant pressure on the system, and even minor errors can lead to potentially catastrophic incidents. The most significant recent event highlighting these risks occurred on April 13, 2023. On that day, Canadian National Railway freight train M 37231-13 passed a Stop signal at Mile 69.4, near Cornwall, Ontario . The train was traveling eastward at a speed of 43.2 mph on the south track when the signal turned red . Moments later, a westbound VIA Rail passenger train, P 06721-13, entered the same section of track, resulting in a near-collision . The incident prompted an immediate and thorough investigation by the Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB). The TSB's final report, released on October 16, 2024, detailed the sequence of events and the contributing factors that led to the signal violation . This event serves as a stark reminder that even in a highly controlled, technologically advanced system, human error and procedural breakdowns remain critical vulnerabilities. It underscores the perpetual challenge of maintaining an impeccable safety record in a corridor that handles a massive volume of high-speed traffic every single day. The incident triggered a renewed focus on safety protocols and dispatch procedures, reflecting the industry-wide imperative to learn from such close calls to prevent future accidents.

The Kingston Subdivision is served by a series of key stations, many of which have evolved over time. The northern terminus is Union Station Rail Corridor in Toronto, a major hub for commuter, intercity, and regional rail services , . Other active stations along the line include Danforth, Scarborough, Whitby, Oshawa, Port Hope, Cobourg, Trenton Junction, Belleville, Napanee, Kingston, Gananoque, Brockville, Cornwall, and the southern terminus at Dorval, just outside of Montreal , . Some stations have been abandoned or repurposed as the region's development patterns have shifted. For instance, Lansdowne station closed in 1966, and Iroquois station was removed in 2002 . In contrast, some historic stations have found new life; Brighton station is now part of the Memory Junction railway museum, and Prescott station is operated by a local historical society, preserving a tangible link to the area's railway heritage . The Kingston Outer Station, however, has been left abandoned and is now in ruins, standing as a physical manifestation of the changing fortunes of rail transport in certain communities . The line's history is also marked by the absorption of smaller, competing railways. For example, the Kingston & Pembroke Railway (K&PR), a line built in the 1870s to connect Kingston with Pembroke, was never completed and instead terminated in Renfrew, where it connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) . The K&PR line was progressively abandoned throughout the latter half of the 20th century, with the final section closing in 1986, illustrating how the dominance of larger systems like CN's can lead to the decline of alternative routes . The Kingston Subdivision, in contrast, has thrived, solidifying its position as a cornerstone of Canada's transportation infrastructure.

## Comparative Analysis and Legacy

The term "Kingston Line," while geographically disparate, encompasses two distinct but thematically resonant pieces of railway infrastructure: the historic, partially derelict network in Kingston, Jamaica, and the modern, high-volume corridor in Kingston, Ontario, Canada. A comparative analysis reveals a fascinating duality: one line represents a legacy of colonial-era development and a contemporary struggle for revival, while the other embodies the pinnacle of 21st-century freight and passenger logistics. Both, however, share overarching narratives of significance, decline, and the enduring human desire to connect places and people. Their legacies are shaped by vastly different contexts—the socio-economic forces of post-colonial Jamaica versus the relentless demands of North American commerce—and their stories offer a compelling lens through which to view the evolution of rail transport on a global scale.

The historical origins of the two lines could not be more different. The Jamaican Kingston Line is a product of the 19th century, born from the ambitions of a British colony seeking to industrialize and integrate its geography , . Its opening in 1845 marked a transformative moment, positioning Kingston as the logical starting point for a national network . In contrast, the Canadian Kingston Subdivision's roots trace back to the mid-19th century as well, but its development was driven by the practical necessity of linking burgeoning cities in a vast, resource-rich nation . While the Jamaican line expanded from a single terminus, the Canadian line was conceived as a grand trunk line from the outset, a decision that gave it a strategic advantage in becoming a primary artery of the continent's rail system. Architecturally, the Jamaican line is notable for its uniform and charming Jamaica/Georgian style, a reflection of its colonial origins . The Canadian line, meanwhile, reflects a more utilitarian approach to industrial engineering, prioritizing functionality and capacity over stylistic flourishes.

The trajectory of decline and revival presents perhaps the most striking divergence between the two entities. The fate of the Jamaican railway system is a classic tale of economic obsolescence. The cessation of passenger service in 1992 was not a planned shutdown but the result of systemic failure—a lack of government funding and waning public interest that rendered the network unviable , . The physical infrastructure fell into a state of dereliction, epitomized by the neglected Kingston Railway Terminus . The push for revival in Jamaica is therefore a deliberate act of reclamation. Led by the Jamaica Railway Corporation and supported by international aid from institutions like the Inter-American Development Bank, the goal is to breathe new life into a decaying asset, framing it as a tool for urban regeneration and sustainable development , , . The focus is on restoring heritage and reconnecting communities.

Conversely, the Kingston Subdivision in Canada is not in decline; rather, it is under immense operational stress. The "revival" here is not about saving a dying institution but about sustaining a vital economic engine. The line is fully operational, carrying a heavy load of freight and passenger traffic every day . Its challenges are not of abandonment but of management. The 2023 signal-passing incident near Cornwall was a stark illustration of the inherent risks in a high-density, high-speed corridor where millions of dollars worth of freight and hundreds of passengers are moved daily . The response to such incidents is not a call for revival but an intensification of safety measures and technological oversight. The legacy of the Canadian line is one of resilience and efficiency, a testament to the success of large-scale infrastructure in meeting the demands of a modern economy. The contrast is clear: Jamaica's challenge is one of rediscovery and reinvestment, while Canada's is one of maintenance and risk mitigation.

Both lines are indelibly marked by significant human events that have shaped their legacies. The Kendal rail disaster of 1957 on the Jamaican line stands as a profound national tragedy, a singular event of immense loss of life that reverberated through the community and likely hastened the end of an era for passenger rail in Jamaica . It is a story of personal and collective grief that gives the line a powerful emotional resonance beyond its logistical function. The Canadian Kingston Subdivision, by contrast, has a history dominated by corporate and regulatory actors. While its 2023 near-miss was a serious incident, it highlights the effectiveness of modern safety systems and the low probability of a similar event occurring again. The legacy of the Canadian line is therefore one of engineering triumph and operational excellence, measured in metrics of efficiency and safety performance rather than in personal stories of tragedy. The human element is present, but it is expressed through the lives of commuters, freight handlers, and engineers who depend on the line's reliability every day.

In conclusion, the term "Kingston Line" encapsulates two fundamentally different chapters in the history of rail transport. The Jamaican Kingston Line is a cultural artifact, a piece of national heritage currently undergoing a process of careful restoration. Its story is one of hope, renewal, and the re-evaluation of a once-central pillar of the nation's infrastructure. The Canadian Kingston Subdivision is an economic powerhouse, a high-tech logistical marvel that is indispensable to the flow of commerce in Eastern Canada. Its story is one of constant adaptation, intense pressure, and the unwavering pursuit of safety in a demanding environment. Together, they demonstrate the diverse roles that railways play in society: as symbols of national identity and progress, as engines of economic growth, and as systems that demand constant vigilance and investment to ensure their safe and effective operation. Understanding these two distinct "Kingston Lines" provides a richer, more nuanced appreciation of the complex and enduring relationship between nations and their rails.

At approximately 11:30 p.m. on September 1, 1957, a train departing Kingston bound for Montego Bay crashed near the village of Kendal.
The Kendal rail disaster resulted in an estimated 200 fatalities.
The Kendal rail disaster resulted in between 400 and 700 injuries.
The Kendal rail disaster was the worst transportation tragedy in Jamaica's history.
At the time, the Kendal rail disaster was the second-worst rail disaster globally.
The Kendal crash stands as a profound turning point.
The Kendal crash likely accelerated the loss of confidence in the railway system.
The Kendal crash contributed significantly to the long-term decline in passenger usage that culminated in the full cessation of services in 1992.
The legacy of the Kendal event underscores the inherent risks of early railway operations.
The legacy of the Kendal event serves as a somber reminder of the human cost associated with the industrialization of transport.
Today, the original Kingston-Spanish Town line, the very first segment of the Kingston Line, survives in a state of partial dereliction but continues to be a focus of preservation efforts.
The Jamaica Community Rail Project (JCRP) is actively working to transform the abandoned station buildings and the surrounding rail line into a tourist attraction.
The Jamaica Community Rail Project (JCRP) is preserving a tangible link to Jamaica's rich railway past.

Stations along this historic route, such as Gregory Park and Grange Lane, and the terminus at Angels’ Halt, remain as silent witnesses to the era of steam and steel that once defined the island's connectivity.
The term "Kingston Line" in a Canadian context refers to the Kingston Subdivision.
The Kingston Subdivision is a major and heavily trafficked railway corridor owned primarily by Canadian National Railway (CN).
The Kingston Subdivision line is a critical artery of North American rail transport.
The Kingston Subdivision serves as the principal high-speed route connecting Toronto's Union Station with Montreal Central Station.
Historically, the Kingston Subdivision originated as the main trunk line of the Grand Trunk Railway in the 1850s.
The Kingston Subdivision established the foundational rail link between Canada's two largest metropolitan areas.
The Kingston Subdivision runs primarily along the north shore of Lake Ontario and the Saint Lawrence River.
The Kingston Subdivision forms a continuous and vital link in the continent's freight and passenger network.
Unlike its Jamaican counterpart, the Kingston Subdivision is a modern, technologically advanced, and economically indispensable asset.
The Kingston Subdivision's operations are characterized by high volumes of both freight and passenger traffic.
The Kingston Subdivision's operations are characterized by sophisticated centralized traffic control.
The Kingston Subdivision's operations are characterized by the ongoing challenges of managing safety within a high-intensity environment.
The Kingston Subdivision's history is intertwined with the consolidation of Canadian railways.
The Kingston Subdivision's present-day narrative is defined by its role in moving essential goods and intercity travelers across one of the world's busiest corridors.
The Kingston Subdivision was originally constructed in the 1850s by the Grand Trunk Railway (GTR) as its main route between Toronto and Montreal.
The Kingston Subdivision's proximity to the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway facilitated the seamless transfer of cargo between rail and marine vessels.
The Kingston Subdivision's proximity to the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway cemented its importance in the national economy.
Over time, the GTR was absorbed by the Canadian National Railway.
Canadian National Railway continues to own and operate the majority of the Kingston Subdivision today.
The ownership structure of the Kingston Subdivision is unique in that it is shared among different operators.
CN owns and operates the section of the Kingston Subdivision east of Pickering Junction, Ontario, all the way to Dorval East in Montréal.
The segment of the Kingston Subdivision from Union Station Rail Corridor in Toronto to Pickering Junction is owned by Metrolinx.
Metrolinx is the regional transportation agency for the Greater Toronto Area.
The Metrolinx portion of the Kingston Subdivision is exclusively used by GO Transit for its Lakeshore East commuter rail service.
VIA Rail, Canada's national passenger train operator, utilizes the entire length of the Kingston Subdivision for its intercity services.
VIA Rail operates trains on both the Toronto-Montreal and Toronto-Ottawa corridors of the Kingston Subdivision.
This multi-operator model makes the Kingston Subdivision a prime example of a shared-use corridor.
The Kingston Subdivision balances the demands of heavy-duty freight, high-frequency commuter transit, and long-distance passenger travel.
Operationally, the Kingston Subdivision is a high-capacity, high-speed rail line engineered for maximum efficiency.
The Kingston Subdivision is a standard gauge line (1,435 mm).
The Kingston Subdivision's standard gauge ensures compatibility with other major North American rail systems.
The Kingston Subdivision consists of two to four main tracks.
The Kingston Subdivision's track configuration allows for the simultaneous passage of trains traveling in opposite directions.
Traffic management on the Kingston Subdivision is handled by a sophisticated Centralized Traffic Control (CTC) system.
The Centralized Traffic Control (CTC) system has been in place on the Kingston Subdivision since 1995.
The CTC technology allows a single traffic controller, based remotely in Edmonton, Alberta, to manage train movements across vast distances.
The CTC technology eliminates the need for traditional block signals and manual clearance forms (OCS).
This level of automation is essential for handling the Kingston Subdivision's substantial daily traffic load.
On average, the Kingston Subdivision carries approximately 18 CN freight trains each day.
On average, the Kingston Subdivision carries approximately 12 VIA passenger trains each day.
Freight operations on the Kingston Subdivision include everything from intermodal containers to bulk commodities.
Passenger services on the Kingston Subdivision range from the high-speed Toronto-Montreal runs to the slower Toronto-Ottawa trains that diverge from the main line at Brockville.
The Kingston Subdivision can accommodate speeds of up to 90 mph for VIA trains.
The Kingston Subdivision can accommodate speeds of 60-90 mph for other passenger services.
The Kingston Subdivision's design allows for high-performance transit.
The complexity of the Kingston Subdivision's mixed-use environment is managed through a network of over 50 interlocking crossover tracks.
Interlocking crossover tracks allow for the efficient interchange of trains, particularly between CN's freight fleet and VIA's passenger fleet.
Despite its technological sophistication and economic importance, the Kingston Subdivision is not immune to operational challenges and safety concerns.
The sheer density of traffic on the Kingston Subdivision creates constant pressure on the system.
Even minor errors on the Kingston Subdivision can lead to potentially catastrophic incidents.
The most significant recent event highlighting these risks occurred on April 13, 2023.
On April 13, 2023, Canadian National Railway freight train M 37231-13 passed a Stop signal at Mile 69.4, near Cornwall, Ontario.
The freight train M 37231-13 was traveling eastward at a speed of 43.2 mph on the south track when the signal turned red.
Moments later, a westbound VIA Rail passenger train, P 06721-13, entered the same section of track, resulting in a near-collision.
The incident prompted an immediate and thorough investigation by the Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB).
The TSB's final report, released on October 16, 2024, detailed the sequence of events and the contributing factors that led to the signal violation.
This event serves as a stark reminder that even in a highly controlled, technologically advanced system, human error and procedural breakdowns remain critical vulnerabilities.
The incident underscores the perpetual challenge of maintaining an impeccable safety record in a corridor that handles a massive volume of high-speed traffic every single day.
The incident triggered a renewed focus on safety protocols and dispatch procedures.
The renewed focus reflects the industry-wide imperative to learn from such close calls to prevent future accidents.
The Kingston Subdivision is served by a series of key stations.
The northern terminus of the Kingston Subdivision is Union Station Rail Corridor in Toronto.
Union Station Rail Corridor is a major hub for commuter, intercity, and regional rail services.

Other active stations along the Kingston Subdivision line include Danforth, Scarborough, Whitby, Oshawa, Port Hope, Cobourg, Trenton Junction, Belleville, Napanee, Kingston, Gananoque, Brockville, Cornwall, and the southern terminus at Dorval, just outside of Montreal.
Some stations along the Kingston Subdivision have been abandoned or repurposed as the region's development patterns have shifted.
Lansdowne station closed in 1966.
Iroquois station was removed in 2002.
Brighton station is now part of the Memory Junction railway museum.
Prescott station is operated by a local historical society.
Prescott station preserves a tangible link to the area's railway heritage.
The Kingston Outer Station has been left abandoned and is now in ruins.
The Kingston Outer Station stands as a physical manifestation of the changing fortunes of rail transport in certain communities.
The Kingston Subdivision's history is also marked by the absorption of smaller, competing railways.
The Kingston & Pembroke Railway (K&PR) was a line built in the 1870s to connect Kingston with Pembroke.
The Kingston & Pembroke Railway (K&PR) was never completed to Pembroke.
The Kingston & Pembroke Railway (K&PR) terminated in Renfrew, where it connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR).
The K&PR line was progressively abandoned throughout the latter half of the 20th century.
The final section of the K&PR line closed in 1986.
The dominance of larger systems like CN's can lead to the decline of alternative routes.
The Kingston Subdivision has thrived, solidifying its position as a cornerstone of Canada's transportation infrastructure.
The Jamaican Kingston Line is a product of the 19th century.
The Jamaican Kingston Line was born from the ambitions of a British colony seeking to industrialize and integrate its geography.
The opening of the Jamaican Kingston Line in 1845 marked a transformative moment.
The opening of the Jamaican Kingston Line in 1845 positioned Kingston as the logical starting point for a national network.
The Canadian Kingston Subdivision's roots trace back to the mid-19th century.
The Canadian Kingston Subdivision's development was driven by the practical necessity of linking burgeoning cities in a vast, resource-rich nation.
While the Jamaican line expanded from a single terminus, the Canadian line was conceived as a grand trunk line from the outset.
The Canadian line's conception as a grand trunk line gave it a strategic advantage in becoming a primary artery of the continent's rail system.
Architecturally, the Jamaican line is notable for its uniform and charming Jamaica/Georgian style.
The Jamaica/Georgian style of the Jamaican line is a reflection of its colonial origins.
The Canadian line reflects a more utilitarian approach to industrial engineering.
The Canadian line prioritizes functionality and capacity over stylistic flourishes.
The fate of the Jamaican railway system is a classic tale of economic obsolescence.
The cessation of passenger service in 1992 on the Jamaican line was not a planned shutdown but the result of systemic failure.
Systemic failure on the Jamaican line included a lack of government funding and waning public interest that rendered the network unviable.
The physical infrastructure of the Jamaican line fell into a state of dereliction.
The dereliction of the Jamaican line's physical infrastructure is epitomized by the neglected Kingston Railway Terminus.
The push for revival in Jamaica is a deliberate act of reclamation.
The push for revival in Jamaica is led by the Jamaica Railway Corporation.
The push for revival in Jamaica is supported by international aid from institutions like the Inter-American Development Bank.
The goal of the Jamaican revival is to breathe new life into a decaying asset.
The Jamaican revival frames the railway as a tool for urban regeneration and sustainable development.
The focus of the Jamaican revival is on restoring heritage and reconnecting communities.
The Kingston Subdivision in Canada is not in decline.
The Kingston Subdivision in Canada is under immense operational stress.
The Kingston Subdivision line is fully operational.
The Kingston Subdivision carries a heavy load of freight and passenger traffic every day.
The challenges of the Canadian Kingston Subdivision are not of abandonment but of management.
The 2023 signal-passing incident near Cornwall was a stark illustration of the inherent risks in a high-density, high-speed corridor.
Millions of dollars worth of freight and hundreds of passengers are moved daily on the Canadian Kingston Subdivision.
The response to such incidents on the Canadian Kingston Subdivision is an intensification of safety measures and technological oversight.
The legacy of the Canadian line is one of resilience and efficiency.
The Canadian line is a testament to the success of large-scale infrastructure in meeting the demands of a modern economy.
Jamaica's challenge is one of rediscovery and reinvestment.
Canada's challenge is one of maintenance and risk mitigation.
The Kendal rail disaster of 1957 on the Jamaican line stands as a profound national tragedy.
The Kendal rail disaster was a singular event of immense loss of life that reverberated through the community.
The Kendal rail disaster likely hastened the end of an era for passenger rail in Jamaica.
The Kendal rail disaster is a story of personal and collective grief that gives the line a powerful emotional resonance beyond its logistical function.
The Canadian Kingston Subdivision has a history dominated by corporate and regulatory actors.
The 2023 near-miss on the Canadian Kingston Subdivision was a serious incident.
The 2023 near-miss highlights the effectiveness of modern safety systems.
The 2023 near-miss highlights the low probability of a similar event occurring again.
The legacy of the Canadian line is one of engineering triumph and operational excellence.
The legacy of the Canadian line is measured in metrics of efficiency and safety performance rather than in personal stories of tragedy.

Bringing the trains back to Kingston
====================================

[WhatsApp](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/#whatsapp) [Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fjamaica-gleaner.com%2Fgleaner%2F20120422%2Flead%2Flead8.html&title=Bringing%20the%20trains%20back%20to%20Kingston%20%7C%20Lead%20Stories%20%7C%20Jamaica%20Gleaner)

Published:Sunday | April 22, 2012 | 12:00 AM

*   [Photo](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/gleaner/20120422/lead/lead8.html?qt-article_image_video=0#qt-article_image_video)
*   [Video](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/gleaner/20120422/lead/lead8.html?qt-article_image_video=1#qt-article_image_video)

![Image 2](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/sites/default/files/styles/jg_article_image/public/article_images/2012/04/22/2.jpg?itok=33tRQ64f)

Residents of Bog Walk, St Catherine, converge at the local train station for a closer view of the reconditioned five-coach train, on its test run from May Pen, Clarendon, to Linstead. - File

Last October, I wrote in this newspaper about a marvellously evocative railway journey I made from Spanish Town to Linstead on the newly restored passenger train service. Let me say, first of all, how pleased I am that this service has been maintained up to now. It is a first, symbolic step towards the restoration of the entire Jamaican railway system.

Following that episode, and being a newcomer to Kingston, I made a point of visiting the now sadly derelict Kingston Railway Terminus, and the thought occurred to me that it would be a tremendous boon to the whole downtown area if the railway were to return to Kingston, with the station as the transportation hub of the city.

The excellent article, 'The Making of a city', recently published on your pages, with which I agree wholeheartedly, reminded me of the importance of the railway to the urban development of Kingston, and to its promotion as a vibrant and beautiful capital city.

The concept of the railway station being the 'centre of the city' is well established in Europe, the continent where railways are woven into the fabric of society, and where railways are regarded as social services in much the same way as schools and hospitals. Take, for example, the Italian city of Bologna, known variously as 'La Rossa' (for its 'red', left-wing politics),'La Dotta' (for the educational renown of its university, the oldest in Europe), or 'La Grassa' (for the richness of its food, including 'spaghetti bolognese'). Travellers to Bologna from abroad may arrive at the airport, where they take a shuttle bus to the city centre (the railway station), and there catch a train to another town, or board a local bus or taxi to a destination elsewhere in the city.

Boost for town life

Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox
---------------------------------

[Sign up for The Gleaner’s morning and evening newsletters.](https://member.jamaica-gleaner.com/subscription/?utm_source=Newsletter&utm_medium=textlink&utm_campaign=NewsletterSignUp)

In the immediate vicinity of the station are innumerable hotels and restaurants, and on Saturday mornings, local football fans congregate at the station to catch trains to other towns for 'away' matches. I use this merely as an example of how a railway terminus can serve as a catalyst for all manner of benefits for the general public, and be regarded as the very 'heart' of a city.

In the same vein, what a pleasure it would be for visitors to Kingston from other towns and villages in Jamaica - from as near as Spanish Town or as far as Montego Bay - to arrive by train, in comfort and without the stress of a long road journey, in the heart of Kingston, from where they could take a bus or a taxi to their ultimate destinations, and return home in the same manner!

There seems no doubt that Kingston would be transformed if the railway trains came back. Let us hope that the Government will find willing foreign investors to assist with that transformation. Such investment may not be easy to obtain at this time but, if the political will is present, who knows what may be achieved?

\- Gilbert Kodilinye

[Canadian National Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_National_Railway "Canadian National Railway")'s **Kingston Subdivision**, or **Kingston Sub** for short, is a major [railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_line "Railway line") connecting [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") with [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") that carries the majority of CN traffic between these points. The line was originally the main trunk for the [Grand Trunk Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Trunk_Railway "Grand Trunk Railway") between these cities, although there has been some realignment of the route between these cities. The majority of the Kingston Sub runs close to the northern bank of [Lake Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Ontario "Lake Ontario") and the [Saint Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River").

The infrastructure consists of twin tracks, on which over 50 pieces of interlocking [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_/(rail_transport/) "Crossover (rail transport)") tracks are grafted all along the subdivision. The extra length of these crossover tracks allows for high speed track interchange. Trains are allowed to change tracks at up to 45 miles per hour. The governing traffic control system is [CTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralized_traffic_control "Centralized traffic control"). Since 1995, no [OCS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_Warrant_Control "Track Warrant Control") operation clearance forms need to be filled by train conductors on the Kingston Subdivision. CTC signals thus provide both permission and authorization for train movements, as is the situation with most main line operation at CN.

Just east of [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle,_Ontario "Newcastle, Ontario"), east of Toronto, the line is joined by the [CP Belleville Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=CP_Belleville_Subdivision&action=edit&redlink=1 "CP Belleville Subdivision (page does not exist)"), [Canadian Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Pacific_Railway "Canadian Pacific Railway")'s similar mainline route. The two remain nearly side-by-side to the east of [Belleville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belleville,_Ontario "Belleville, Ontario"), where the Belleville sub turns north to [Smiths Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smiths_Falls,_Ontario "Smiths Falls, Ontario"). Sections of the Kingston Sub are no longer owned by CN. In particular, CN mainline freight traffic in the Toronto area no longer follows the Kingston Sub, and is re-directed north of the city along the [York Sub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_York_Subdivision "CN York Subdivision"). The section between Pickering Junction and [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Toronto/) "Union Station (Toronto)") in downtown Toronto has been sold to [Metrolinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrolinx "Metrolinx") for [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit") service, part of their [Lakeshore East line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeshore_East_line "Lakeshore East line").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-1)

Via rail of Canada operates their corridor service along the entirety of the line. VIAs Toronto-Ottawa trains runs along the line to Brockville, where it splits off and heads north. The Toronto-Montreal train runs along the whole line. In fact, many say that VIA trains run along the line more than CN freight trains. The most used station on the line is Kingston, due to Montreal, and Toronto stations being on their own subdivisions.

The Kingston subdivision primarily runs along the north shore of Lake Ontario. From Toronto's Union station to Pickering junction, in west Pickering, where the Kingston sub intersects with the York sub, the line is known as the “GO Kingston sub”. Between Union and Pickering junction, the line is triple tracked. Leaving Union station's rail corridor, the line is intersected by the CN Bala subdivision, before curving slightly north, through the south end of Toronto's east York community. The first stop outside of union, is Danforth, just off Danforth Rd. GO lakeshore east trains stop, and VIA trains don't. From there, the line passes Scarborough station, off Saint Claire Ave, and just east of Scarborough the GO Stouffville line splits off. The Kingston sub then passes rouge hill, Guildwood, and Eglington stations, before reaching Pickering junction, where the GO trains are split and run parallel to the Kingston sub. From Pickering junction to Dorval, the line is known as the CN Kingston sub. Between Pickering junction and Oshawa GO, where the lakeshore east line ends, the Kingston sub runs through the cities of Whitby, Pickering, Ajax, and Oshawa. However, the Kingston sub only has a station in Oshawa, because CN and VIA trains are ran along the Kingston sub, which only has a station in Oshawa, while GO trains run along a parallel set of tracks, and stop at Pickering Ajax and Whitby. Between Oshawa GO and Darlington provincial park in west Bowmanville, the tracks run side by side with the highway 401. From Darlington park, it curves slightly running just to the north of Darlington nuclear generating station. From there, curves north again, between Bowmanville and Newcastle, and runs alongside the 401 again for a short time. From Newcastle, it weaves its way between Lake Ontario and highway 401, to port hope in west Northumberland county. From there, the Kingston sub runs through Cobourg, and between Cobourg and Belleville, runs parallel to, but slightly north of Lake Ontario. East of Belleville and Hastings county, the line travels farther inland, to Napanee. Just east of Napanee, the line once again parallels Lake Ontario, with some final curves before Kingston. From Kingston, the line passes north of highway 401, through the communities of Landsdowne, Gananoque, and Mallorytown, before passing again under the 401, into Brockville. Between Brockville and Cornwall, the Kingston sub runs parallel to the st Lawrence river, passing through the communities of Prescott and Maitland, before arriving in Cornwall. East of Cornwall, the line passes once again under the 401, bringing it into the small town of Le Coteau. From there, the line remains alongside Quebec autoroute 20, before ending in Dorval, just outside of Montreal.

The 1850s [Grand Trunk Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Trunk_Railway "Grand Trunk Railway") mainline consisted of 34 stations, many of which have been removed from service or no longer exist. [Lansdowne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lansdowne,_Ontario "Lansdowne, Ontario") station was torn down soon after CN abandoned service to the village in 1966;[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-2) CN demolished an [Iroquois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois,_Ontario "Iroquois, Ontario") station in 2002.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-3)

Stations currently on the Toronto-Montréal mainline include:

*   [Union Station (Toronto)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Toronto/) "Union Station (Toronto)")
*   [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit") (no VIA service) at [Danforth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danforth_GO_Station "Danforth GO Station"), [Scarborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_GO_Station "Scarborough GO Station"), [Eglinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eglinton_GO_Station "Eglinton GO Station") in Toronto
*   [Guildwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildwood_GO_Station "Guildwood GO Station")
*   Commuter stations in [Rouge Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouge_Hill_GO_Station "Rouge Hill GO Station")/[Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickering_GO_Station "Pickering GO Station"), [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajax_GO_Station "Ajax GO Station") and [Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitby_GO_Station "Whitby GO Station") serve [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit"); No VIA service
*   [Oshawa GO Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oshawa_GO_Station "Oshawa GO Station")
*   [Port Hope railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Hope_railway_station "Port Hope railway station")
*   [Cobourg railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobourg_railway_station "Cobourg railway station")
*   Brighton (not in use, was part of [Memory Junction railway museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_Junction_railway_museum "Memory Junction railway museum")[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-4))
*   [Trenton Junction railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton_Junction_railway_station "Trenton Junction railway station")
*   [Belleville station (Ontario)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belleville_station_/(Ontario/) "Belleville station (Ontario)")
*   [Napanee railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napanee_railway_station "Napanee railway station")
*   [Ernestown (not in use)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernestown_Railway_Station "Ernestown Railway Station")
*   [Kingston railway station (Ontario)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station_/(Ontario/) "Kingston railway station (Ontario)")
*   Kingston Outer Station (abandoned, in ruins[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-5))
*   [Gananoque railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gananoque_railway_station "Gananoque railway station")
*   [Brockville railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockville_railway_station "Brockville railway station")
*   Prescott (not in use, now houses Grenville historical society and archives)
*   Morrisburg (abandoned in 2020[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#cite_note-6)}
*   [Cornwall railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall_railway_station "Cornwall railway station")
*   [Dorval railway station (Via)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorval_railway_station_/(Via/) "Dorval railway station (Via)")
*   The line ended at [Bonaventure Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonaventure_Station_/(1887%E2%80%931952/) "Bonaventure Station (1887–1952)"), which has been replaced by [Montreal Central Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Central_Station "Montreal Central Station").

[Thousands of fans join tribute to reggae pioneer Jimmy Cliff in his native Jamaica](https://www.britannica.com/news/318748/89b2e8a9c7acc10eb5dafae94899eed3) • Dec. 17, 2025, 6:13 PM ET (AP) ...(Show more)

Show less

**Kingston**, city, capital, and chief port of [Jamaica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Jamaica), sprawling along the southeastern coast of the island, backed by the [Blue Mountains](https://www.britannica.com/place/Blue-Mountains-Jamaica). It is famous for its fine natural harbour, which is protected by the Palisadoes, a narrow peninsula that has been developed as a recreational and tourist resort.

Kingston was founded in 1692 after [Port Royal](https://www.britannica.com/place/Port-Royal-Jamaica), at the mouth of the harbour, was destroyed by an [earthquake](https://www.britannica.com/science/earthquake-geology). The core of the old city is a consciously planned rectangle with streets in a grid pattern. In 1703 the city became the commercial capital, and in 1872 the political capital, of Jamaica. On several occasions it was almost destroyed by fire, and in January 1907 it suffered a violent earthquake.

[![Image 16: Rockfort, Kingston, Jamaica](https://cdn.britannica.com/10/42610-004-BBC931E1/Rockfort-Kingston-Jam.jpg?w=400&h=225&c=crop) 1 of 2](https://cdn.britannica.com/10/42610-004-BBC931E1/Rockfort-Kingston-Jam.jpg)

[Rockfort, Kingston, Jamaica](https://cdn.britannica.com/10/42610-004-BBC931E1/Rockfort-Kingston-Jam.jpg)Rockfort, a moated fortress at Kingston, Jamaica.(more)

 [![Image 17: How Bob Marley brought reggae into the mainstream](https://cdn.britannica.com/18/253118-138-59D6890F/bob-marley-jamaican-singer-songwriter-rastafarian-reggae-ska-rock-steady.jpg?w=800&h=450&c=crop) 2 of 2](https://www.britannica.com/video/bob-marley-jamaican-singer-songwriter-rastafarian-reggae-ska-rock-steady/-296916)

How Bob Marley brought reggae into the mainstreamOverview of Bob Marley's career, including footage of the One Love concert, which has been called the “Jamaican Woodstock.” (more)

[See all videos for this article](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kingston-Jamaica/images-videos)

In the main streets of the city, modern buildings contrast sharply with the [decaying](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/decaying) architectural relics of former centuries. The Church of [St. Thomas](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Thomas), on King Street, the chief thoroughfare, was first built before 1699 but was rebuilt after the earthquake in 1907. At the eastern limits of the town stands [Rockfort](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rockfort), a moated fortress dating from the late 17th century and last manned in 1865. On Duke Street stands Headquarters House (formerly the seat of government), built by Thomas Hibbert, an 18th-century merchant; it is one of the few remaining architectural showpieces of a city once renowned for its fine houses. The Institute of Jamaica on East Street maintains a public library, museum, and art gallery especially devoted to local interests. The University of the [West Indies](https://www.britannica.com/place/West-Indies-island-group-Atlantic-Ocean) (founded 1948) is at Mona, 5 miles (8 km) from Kingston’s city centre. The Royal [Botanical](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Botanical) Gardens are at nearby Hope.

[![Image 18: Pakistan Monument is a landmark in Islamabad which represents the four provinces of Pakistan.](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/215483-131-BD51CA13/Pakistan-Monument-landmark-Islamabad-Pakistan.jpg) Britannica Quiz Countries and Capitals Quiz](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/countries-and-capitals-quiz)

[![Image 19: Kingston, Jamaica](https://cdn.britannica.com/17/244317-050-4E042C2C/Locator-map-Kingston.jpg?w=400&h=225&c=crop)](https://cdn.britannica.com/17/244317-050-4E042C2C/Locator-map-Kingston.jpg)

[Kingston, Jamaica](https://cdn.britannica.com/17/244317-050-4E042C2C/Locator-map-Kingston.jpg)(more)

By the 1980s most of the old wharves had been demolished and the entire waterfront redeveloped with hotels, shops, offices, a cultural centre, and cruise and cargo ship facilities. The airport at Palisadoes has domestic and international service. A government-owned railway ran from Kingston to most of Jamaica’s 14 parishes over 210 miles (340 km) of track until 1992, when operation ceased because of lack of funding and low passenger usage. A few rail lines still function to transport bauxite.

Since 1923 the small parish of the original Kingston has merged physically and administratively with [St. Andrew](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Andrew) parish. More than one-quarter of the population of the whole country lives within the boundaries of the Kingston and St. Andrew Corporation. Pop. (2011) Kingston and St. Andrew Corporation, 662,426.

**Kingston railway terminus** was built in the [Jamaica Georgian architectural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Georgian_architecture "Jamaican Georgian architecture") style using brick.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-jnht-2) It was constructed on a grand scale, symbolising its importance as the main terminus of the Jamaica railways.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-jnht-2) It has prominent arcades on both levels of the east entrance end.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-jnht-2) Victorian cast iron brackets support the roof overhang on the trackside.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-jnht-2) It has [sash windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sash_window "Sash window") on the ground and upper floors.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-jnht-2)

It was opened in 1845 and closed in 1992.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH18-1) It provided rail services to [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railways_of_Jamaica:_Kingston_to_Montego_Bay "Railways of Jamaica: Kingston to Montego Bay"), [Port Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railways_of_Jamaica:_Bog_Walk_to_Port_Antonio "Railways of Jamaica: Bog Walk to Port Antonio"), [Ewarton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railways_of_Jamaica:_Spanish_Town_to_Ewarton "Railways of Jamaica: Spanish Town to Ewarton") and [Frankfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railways_of_Jamaica:_May_Pen_to_Frankfield "Railways of Jamaica: May Pen to Frankfield"). In addition to the station and its single platform there were extensive [sidings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siding_/(rail/) "Siding (rail)"), engine sheds, engine repair works, a [roundhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_roundhouse "Railway roundhouse"), a [turntable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_turntable "Railway turntable"), a [traverser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_table "Transfer table") and a connection to the nearby railway piers.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-3)

One source claims it was "utterly destroyed" in the [1907 Kingston earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1907_Kingston_earthquake "1907 Kingston earthquake").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-4) However, in 2003 it was reported as being in "very good condition" and needing only "minor repairs".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-TSR-5)

It is on the [list of designated National Heritage Sites in Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Heritage_Sites_in_Jamaica "List of National Heritage Sites in Jamaica").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica#cite_note-6)

| The **Kingston to Montego Bay railway** was the main [railway in Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica "Rail transport in Jamaica"), which from 1845 to 1992 linked the capital [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Jamaica "Kingston, Jamaica") with the second city [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay"), passing en route most of the major towns. Construction, operation and closure ----------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Construction, operation and closure")\] The first 14.5 miles (23.3 km) of 4 ft 8+1⁄2 in (1,435 mm) ([standard gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gauge "Standard gauge")) track were laid from Kingston to Angels (just north of [Spanish Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Town "Spanish Town")) in 1845 at a cost of £222,250, or £15,377 per mile against a budgeted cost £150,000.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-JTH1-3) An 11-mile (18 km) extension from [Spanish Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Town "Spanish Town") to [Old Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Harbour,_Jamaica "Old Harbour, Jamaica") was added in 1869[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-JTH3-4) at a cost of £60,000.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-Fox-5) A further 24.5 miles (39.4 km) extension from [Old Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Harbour,_Jamaica "Old Harbour, Jamaica") to [Porus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porus,_Jamaica "Porus, Jamaica") was added in 1885 at a cost of around £187,000.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-Fox-5) The final 62 miles (100 km) from [Porus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porus,_Jamaica "Porus, Jamaica") to [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay") was completed in 1895.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DiscJam5-6) Much of the line closed in October 1992 when all passenger traffic on Jamaica's railways abruptly ceased. Some sections remain in use for [bauxite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauxite "Bauxite") and [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") freight[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-JTH18-7) while the section from Montego Bay to the Appleton Estate remained open for a while as a [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_railway "Heritage railway"). Gradients and curvature ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Gradients and curvature")\] From Kingston the line ran west along the coastal plain, within 50 feet (15.2 m) of sea level, for about 40 miles (64 km) before starting a gentle climb over 5.25 miles (8.45 km) from Bodles to 250 feet (76.2 m) near Lancaster Halt.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) From here there was a plateau for about 24.25 miles (39.03 km) to the Milk River and the start of the 20 miles (32 km) climb through Scotts Pass and Porus to 1,500 feet (457.2 m) just north of Kendal.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) Between Kendal and Mile Gully the line reaches its summit at around 1,700 feet (518.2 m); in this section the [ruling curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruling_curvature "Ruling curvature") was 300 feet (91.4 m) and the ruling [gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_/(slope/) "Grade (slope)") was 1 in 30 (3.33%).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-RM-8) From Mile Gully there was a gentle descent over 17 miles (27 km) to 500 feet (152.4 m) near Raheen.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) From here the line ran on the level across the Appleton Plain to Maggotty and the start of a climb to 1,000 feet (304.8 m) near Stonehenge.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) From here to Catadupa the line ran on the level then descended to 500 feet (152.4 m) at Seven River.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) Another level section brought it to Long Hill Tunnel and the final descent into Montego Bay.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1) There were 22 stations and 17 halts:[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-DoOS-1)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway#cite_note-mtw03/04-9)

![Image 1: Card Image](https://mtm.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/JRC_intro_img.jpg)

**Vision & Mission Statement**
------------------------------

Restore. Modernize. Expand.

To recommence a safe, reliable and affordable freight and passenger rail service throughout Jamaica, to synchronize with other modes of transportation, with emphasis on the cost effective movement, while meeting the needs of the JRC, its customers and stakeholders in an environmentally friendly atmosphere, always striving to develop the communities served.

![Image 2: Jamaica Railway Corporation Board of Directors](https://i0.wp.com/mtm.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/JRC_board.png?resize=1024%2C678&ssl=1)

**Jamaica Railway Corporation’s Board of Directors**  
L-R (Front) Ann Marie Heron, Ferris Ziadie (Chairman), Ann Marie Chin  
L-R (Back) Keith Murray, John Rosen, George Clue, Fitzroy Williams (Chief Executive Officer), David Allen, Christopher Leckie

**Brief History of the Jamaican Railway**
-----------------------------------------

The Jamaican railway originated as a private and comparatively small undertaking in 1843, when the Smith’s Brother (William and David) proposed to construct a rail system, which was favourably received by the House of Assembly. Construction commenced in 1844 under the name Railway Company.

The Jamaican railway system was the first railway opened to traffic outside Europe and North America, and the second British Colony after Canada, only twenty (20) years after operations in the United Kingdom.

The operative factors influencing demands for railway construction initially seem to have been the concern and optimism of its promoters (the Smith’s Brothers), and the effect that the railway would have on the economy and society in general.

The first railway locomotives (steam) to be seen in Jamaica arrived and were christened “Projector” and “Patriot”. These pioneer locomotives were followed shortly by others which were named “Emancipation”, “Perseverance”, and “Success.”

After 34 years (1845 – 1879) and 24.25miles/41.0km of railtrack, the Jamaica Government purchased the railway from the Railway Company ending the first phase of the railway history under private management.

Between 1879 and 1900, management/operating the railway system was by the Jamaican Government and an American consortia (The West India Improvement Company), whereby 160miles/255.8km of railtrack was constructed, linking three (3) major ports, in Kingston, Port Antonio, and Montego Bay.

In 1900, as a fully Jamaica Government owned entity, operating as the Jamaica Government Railway, 34.5 miles/55.5 km of rail track was constructed, linking the US Air Base in Vernamfield, Clarendon.  
The Jamaican rail transportation system marked the dawn of innovation involved significant implications for the economy and society in general.

Nevertheless, it can be justifiable that there has since been subsequent periods of its history when the contributions of the railway to the Jamaican society and economy have exceeded the relatively limited expectations of its early promoters.

Its major role, initially was the mass transportation of goods and people. The subsequent railtrack extended throughout the island, allowed more access to the fertile interior areas where the agriculture industries need support, which effected closer social and economic integration and extended domestic markets.  
The discovery of bauxite deposits in the 1940s, brought about the relative need to utilized railway as the preferred mode of transporting the bauxite extract to be processed and shipped.

In 1992, public rail transport services ceased operating, although bauxite industry continue to operate, in part using the JRC lines.

The railway is poised to command a major role in the development of an integrated National Transport System, which will significantly reduce the carnage and congestion on the nation’s roads, while enhancing production in the offering of a safe, reliable, and viable transportation alternative.

To-date, plans are being pursued to rehabilitate the railway network, and increase mobility for the country to compete more effective in a continually changing global market.

Privatisation of The Jamaica Railway Corporation
------------------------------------------------

![Image 3: Parked yellow train with people walking next to it](https://i0.wp.com/mtm.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/JRC_photo1.jpg?ssl=1)

The Government of Jamaica (GOJ) has been actively pursuing efforts for the privatisation of rail services since the cessation of the services in 1992.

The main objective of the privatization was to identify a private sector investor with adequate financial capacity to undertake the rehabilitation, operations, management and maintenance of rail transportation in Jamaica without significant financial support from the GOJ.

Towards this end, there were negotiations over the years with Indian, Canadian, Chinese and American investors who all expressed interest in rehabilitating the railway. However, these negotiations did not advance to the stage of project implementation.

The Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC) proposed an alternative solution for the build-out of the railway service. The Cabinet duly considered and approved the recommended new arrangement for the resuscitation of the railway. Acting in accordance with Cabinet Decision No. 43/17 dated November 20, 2017, the JRC identified a Jamaican group of investors or Consortium led by Mr. Adam Stewart to participate as Joint Venture (JV) partners in the Phase 1 Railway Rehabilitation Plan for Appleton to Montego Bay.

The JRC and the Consortium signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on March 23, 2018 which provides for the finalisation of Technical and Financial Plans within six (6) months of the signing of the MOU.  
It is anticipated that the parties will negotiate and enter into a JV Agreement to facilitate the investment and the associated works to implement the project.

JRC to commence rail service expansion
======================================

Published:Friday | July 12, 2024 | 12:07 AM

*   [Photo](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/article/news/20240712/jrc-commence-rail-service-expansion?qt-article_image_video=0#qt-article_image_video)

![Image 2: A passenger train on a test run from Spanish Town to Linstead in St Catherine.](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/sites/default/files/styles/jg_article_image/public/media/article_images/2024/07/12/2867089/8062918.jpg?itok=ZeF5_L-0)

[Contributed](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/authors/contributed-0)

A passenger train on a test run from Spanish Town to Linstead in St Catherine.

THE JAMAICA Railway Corporation (JRC) is looking to commence work towards launching phase one of the tourist train service between Montpelier, St James,and Appleton Estate in St Elizabeth.

This engagement will involve, among other things, track reconstruction, acquisition of trains and constructing necessary infrastructure along the route.

The corporation also plans to kick-start preparations for the launch of passenger and freight train services between Spanish Town and Kingston.

Additionally, the company will finalise the rollout of commercial rail service from Bodles Junction to Linstead in St Catherine, specifically for transporting aggregates.

These activities form part of the JRC’s programmed continuation this year of strategies targeting the entity’s improved positioning to revitalise and expand rail service and optimise its financial performance.

Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox
---------------------------------

[Sign up for The Gleaner’s morning and evening newsletters.](https://member.jamaica-gleaner.com/subscription/?utm_source=Newsletter&utm_medium=textlink&utm_campaign=NewsletterSignUp)

Details of these and other engagements are contained in the Jamaica Public Bodies of Estimates and Expenditure for the Fiscal Year ending 2024/25.

The JRC is also expected to commence discussions with private investors to secure funding for building rail infrastructure, rehabilitating existing rolling stock, acquiring new trains and upgrading the entity’s Kingston workshop.

Meanwhile, the entity plans to continue the monetisation of real estate properties owned, to generate optimum returns on the portfolio.

The corporation is also looking to expand its leased lands and properties, while considering the implementation of a cashless rental collection system for tenants.

The JRC is a statutory body formed under the Jamaica Railway Corporation Act of 1960.
