From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Kingston_Railway_Station_2007.png/250px-Kingston_Railway_Station_2007.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kingston_Railway_Station_2007.png)

[Kingston railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica "Kingston railway station, Jamaica"), closed since 1992, as seen in 2007

The first railways of Jamaica were constructed from 1845, making it the second [British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") to receive a railway system, following Canada in 1836 with the [Champlain and St Lawrence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champlain_and_St_Lawrence_Railroad "Champlain and St Lawrence Railroad").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JNHT1-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-2) Construction started only twenty years after the [Stockton & Darlington Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockton_%26_Darlington_Railway "Stockton & Darlington Railway") commenced operations in the United Kingdom.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

The public passenger railway service in [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica"), which ended in October 1992,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) had a [brief revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#Revival) in 2011 only to be closed once again in August 2012.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JG20120814-4) The [Parliament of Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Jamaica "Parliament of Jamaica") had supported a revival under a public joint venture corporation with an offshore partner.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-5) Private freight transport continues on limited tracks leading to the various [docks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dock_/(maritime/) "Dock (maritime)") around the island, transporting [bauxite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauxite "Bauxite") and [sugar cane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_cane "Sugar cane") for export.

### 1845 to World War II

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rail_transport_in_Jamaica&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1845 to World War II")\]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Opening_of_the_Jamaica_Railway_-_Kingston_Terminus.jpg/250px-Opening_of_the_Jamaica_Railway_-_Kingston_Terminus.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Opening_of_the_Jamaica_Railway_-_Kingston_Terminus.jpg)

Opening of the Jamaica Railway - [Kingston Terminus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_railway_station,_Jamaica "Kingston railway station, Jamaica")

The first railway, the **Western Jamaica Connecting Railway**, was built in 1845 from Kingston 23.3 kilometres (14.5 mi) to Angels near [Spanish Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Town "Spanish Town").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) The railway was proposed and started by William Smith, originally from [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") who owned land in Jamaica, and his sugar planter brother David.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

The system approved by the Assembly of Jamaica in 1843 was for a double track between Kingston and Spanish Town, with branch lines to Angels, [Port Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Henderson "Port Henderson") and the [Caymanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Caymanas&action=edit&redlink=1 "Caymanas (page does not exist)") sugar estate.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) On 21 November 1845 the Governor of Jamaica [James Bruce, 8th Earl of Elgin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bruce,_8th_Earl_of_Elgin "James Bruce, 8th Earl of Elgin") and ten carriages of passengers, pulled by the company's two locomotives _Projector_ and _Patriot_ built by [Sharp Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharp_Brothers "Sharp Brothers") of [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), travelled 19 kilometres (12 mi) from Kingston to [Spanish Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Town "Spanish Town").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TRM-6) The first train came after the British Government had enacted the [Sugar Duties Act 1846](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Duties_Act_1846 "Sugar Duties Act 1846") and just after the emancipation of slaves, meaning the sugar industry needed the efficiency that the railway would bring to the island.

The construction of the first single-track section was budgeted to cost [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_sterling "Pound sterling")150,000, but cost £222,250, or £15,377 per kilometre (£24,747 per mile). As a result of the cost of building and a downturn in the sugar industry, only another 18 kilometres (11 mi) were added until 1869 in the form of an extension from Spanish Town to [Old Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Harbour,_Jamaica "Old Harbour, Jamaica")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) at a cost of £60,000.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TRM-6)

### Spanish Town to Ewarton railway

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rail_transport_in_Jamaica&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Spanish Town to Ewarton railway")\]

After a period of decline, the new Governor [Sir Anthony Musgrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Musgrave "Anthony Musgrave") agreed a deal in 1879 to buy the existing 42 kilometres (26 mi) of the system for £93,932.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-DiscJam5-7) After an investment and improvement programme, the expansion of the citrus and banana industries led to two extensions, extending the total system to 105 kilometres (65 mi): westward from Old Harbour to [Porus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porus,_Jamaica "Porus, Jamaica") (39.4 kilometres (24.5 mi));[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TRM-6) northwards from Angel to the interior district of [Ewarton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewarton "Ewarton")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-DiscJam5-7) (22.93 kilometres (14.25 mi)).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TRM-6) Both were completed in 1885 at a total cost of approximately £280,000[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TRM-6)

### Bog Walk to Port Antonio

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rail_transport_in_Jamaica&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Bog Walk to Port Antonio")\]

After debates about extensions, on 1 January 1890 the railway was transferred to an American consortium headed by [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") merchant [Frederick Wesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Wesson&action=edit&redlink=1 "Frederick Wesson (page does not exist)"), and extensions from Porus 100 kilometres (62 mi) to [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay") in 1895,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-DiscJam5-7) and an extension through the banana, [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacao_bean "Cacao bean"), citrus and [coconut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut "Coconut") districts of St Catherine, St Mary and Portland was developed over 87 kilometres (54 mi) from [Bog Walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bog_Walk "Bog Walk") to [Port Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Antonio "Port Antonio") in 1896.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-DiscJam5-7) The Jamaican system now had a total of 298 kilometres (185 mi) of railway lines stretching from the south-eastern to the north-western and north-eastern ends of the island.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

### Jamaica Railway Corporation

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rail_transport_in_Jamaica&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Jamaica Railway Corporation")\]

The loans taken out to secure railway ownership by the company, together with its purchase of 308 square kilometres (76,000 acres) of prime Crown land in various parts of Jamaica, proved too strenuous. After defaulting in 1897 and 1898, by order of the Jamaican Supreme Court the company fell into receivership. In 1900 the government assumed responsibility for the railway again, and made it a department of government. It appointed a Railway Advisory Board in 1902 to advise, which remained in place until 1960 when the statutory 100% government owned [J$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_dollar "Jamaican dollar")6million company the **Jamaica Railway Corporation** was created.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Map_of_the_Jamaica_railway_system_at_its_pre-bauxite_peak_%281945%29_-_small_borders.png/250px-Map_of_the_Jamaica_railway_system_at_its_pre-bauxite_peak_%281945%29_-_small_borders.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_the_Jamaica_railway_system_at_its_pre-bauxite_peak_/(1945/)_-_small_borders.png)

Map of the Jamaica railway system at its pre-bauxite peak c. 1945

Between 1900 and 1950, less than 80 kilometres (50 mi) of track was added, mainly to support opening of the interior to banana cultivation:[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

*   1911 - [May Pen to Frankfield railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Pen_to_Frankfield_railway "May Pen to Frankfield railway"): 21-kilometre (13 mi) branch off the Montego Bay line, from [May Pen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Pen "May Pen") to [Chapelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapelton,_Jamaica "Chapelton, Jamaica"), completed in 1913 and extended in 1925 by 16 kilometres (10 mi) to [Frankfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfield "Frankfield").
*   1921 - Linstead to New Works railway: 4.8 kilometres (3 mi) from [Linstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linstead "Linstead") to [New Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_Works&action=edit&redlink=1 "New Works (page does not exist)"), opened on the Bog Walk to Ewarton extension.
*   1942 - in support of military needs for [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), a 10.5-kilometre (6.5 mi) branch line from Logan's Junction near May Pen, to the US military base at [Fort Simmonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fort_Simmonds&action=edit&redlink=1 "Fort Simmonds (page does not exist)") in [Vernamfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernamfield "Vernamfield"). The British government purchased four [USATC S161 Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USATC_S160_Class "USATC S160 Class") to provide transport for the military base.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-Poland1-8) After the line closed in 1956, these were subsumed by JRC.

In the 1940s deposits of bauxite were discovered in the interior, and companies developed both interconnected as well as independent lines to extract, process and ship the minerals:[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

*   [Alcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcan "Alcan") - used the JRC lines from [Bodles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodles,_Jamaica "Bodles, Jamaica") to ship its product to [Port Esquivel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Esquivel "Port Esquivel"), completing 5 kilometres (3 mi) of lines in 1951
*   [Alcoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoa "Alcoa") - built an 31-kilometre (19 mi) railway in 1962 to connect its Woodside mines with the port at [Rocky Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Point,_Jamaica "Rocky Point, Jamaica") Port. It was leased to the JRC; Alcoa provided locomotives, rolling stock and its staff operated and maintained the line under JRC management
*   [Kaiser Bauxite Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kaiser_Bauxite_Company&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kaiser Bauxite Company (page does not exist)") - built 19 kilometres (12 mi) of independent track and 12.1 kilometres (7.5 mi) of sidings running from mines in upper [Saint Ann Parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Ann_Parish,_Jamaica "Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica") to [Discovery Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Bay,_Jamaica "Discovery Bay, Jamaica"). The company tended to run [Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldwin_Locomotive_Works "Baldwin Locomotive Works") locomotives, and purchased eight between 1952 and 1971.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-9)
*   [Alpart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpart "Alpart") - built 18 kilometres (11 mi) of independent track in the 1970s to connect its refinery at [Nain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nain,_Jamaica "Nain, Jamaica") with [Port Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Port_Kaiser&action=edit&redlink=1 "Port Kaiser (page does not exist)") near [Alligator Pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator_Pond "Alligator Pond")
*   Reynolds - built a short independent railway to link mines, drying plants and ports
*   [Windalco](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Windalco&action=edit&redlink=1 "Windalco (page does not exist)")\- Bauxite Line

The agricultural driven growth of the railways was created by the harsh interior geography, and developing consumer needs meant that bananas had to be on a ship within two days of cutting. Shipping rose from 330,000 stems in 1880 to 24 million stems in 1930; then a decline in the industry ended rail transport of bananas by 1969. In 1895 Jamaica had exported 97 million fruits; by 1940 the figure had fallen to 40 million, and after the loss of the monopoly of the British market and the 1951 hurricane it was 5 million in 1975. Passenger use fell, partly because of the bridge-building programme begun by the government before the war. By 1971 Jamaica had 11,590 kilometres (7,200 mi) of roads, 1,350 of which were paved; alongside motorbuses which were accessing further inland, private cars had increased from 15,000 in 1950 to 142,300 in 1975.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

After a post-war report by C. E. Rooke recommended closure of the Port Antonio to Spanish Town line, the government only closed the Linstead to Ewarton branch in 1947.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) The 1951 hurricane brought about a recommendation by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") envoy to invest in the railway to keep the bauxite traffic, and hence the passenger rates, economically viable.

Jamaica Railway Corporation
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rail_transport_in_Jamaica&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Jamaica Railway Corporation")\]

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Jamaican_railroad_with_railcar_and_station_1960.jpg/250px-Jamaican_railroad_with_railcar_and_station_1960.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jamaican_railroad_with_railcar_and_station_1960.jpg)

A motorized railcar leaving [Buff Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buff_Bay "Buff Bay") station, in 1960

The government agreed change of the railway after the 1 September 1957 crash, the worst transport accident in Jamaica's history, in which a 12-car wooden body train carrying 1,600 passengers derailed at Kendal, killing 175 passengers and injuring over 800.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH12-10)

The first diesel power had entered Jamaica in 1939 with two [D Wickham & Co](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D_Wickham_%26_Co "D Wickham & Co") diesel coaches. After the creation of the **Jamaica Railway Corporation** in 1960, management increased this transformation significantly from 1963 onwards:

*   19 multi-unit [Metro-Cammell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Cammell "Metro-Cammell") railcars, powered by [Rolls-Royce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolls-Royce_Limited "Rolls-Royce Limited") C6T Mark IV engines of 260 kW (350 hp) acquired at for J$621,000. These were all composite in two formations, with 7 cars carrying 20 first-class and 58 second-class passengers; and 30 cars with 83 second-class passengers
*   The unique "market car wheel" built by Metro-Cammell, a modified boxcar fitted to carry passengers and their goods to market
*   Two [Clayton Equipment Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Equipment_Company "Clayton Equipment Company") shunting locomotives with the same Rolls-Royce driving system as the Metro-Cammell boxcars
*   Two [English Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric "English Electric") 750 h.p. locomotives to handle bauxite traffic
*   Steam traction ended in 1964 but in 1966 class M3 4-8-0 No.54 was restored to working order for use on special excursion trains, the first one of which was named The Banana Boat Steam Train which ran between Kingston and Port Antonio on 17 July 1966.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-11) "Engine 54" was celebrated in a song by that title released in 1968 by [The Ethiopians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethiopians "The Ethiopians"), one of the leading Jamaican musical groups of the [Rocksteady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocksteady "Rocksteady") era.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-12)

In 1967, two ALCO DL532 1,200 h.p. diesel-electric locomotives were purchased. By 1970 Jamaica's railways had fourteen diesel-electric locomotives and only one steam locomotive was still in operation.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) Between 1972 and 1976, an additional 18 [ALCO RS-8s](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ALCO_RS-8&action=edit&redlink=1 "ALCO RS-8 (page does not exist)"), manufactured by [Montreal Locomotive Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Locomotive_Works "Montreal Locomotive Works") in Canada, were purchased in three batches of six locomotives.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-13)

By 1975 there were:[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-CMM-14)

*   348.4 kilometres (216.5 mi) of 1,435 mm (4 ft 8+1⁄2 in) ([standard gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gauge "Standard gauge")) in control of JRC[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)
*   47 kilometres (29 mi) of private industrial railways in Jamaica.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)
*   Totalling 370 kilometres (230 mi)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-CMM-14)
*   Carrying 1.2 million passengers per annum[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)
*   Transporting 900 million tonnes of goods, 95% bauxite and alumina which had driven the shippage from 900,000 tonnes in 1959.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

By 1973 JRC's operational deficit had risen to J$3.4 million, and in 1975 it was nearing J$4 million and carrying a J$11 million loan. The government was paying over J$1.4 million in subsidy to keep the island's trains running. The financial crisis had led to a backlog of deferred maintenance, with stock and buildings also neglected. In 1974 the May Pen-Frankfield line closed, with the Bog Walk-Port Antonio line closing in 1975.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

Public pressure forced the government to reopen the Port Antonio line at a cost of J$1.4 million in 1977. The condition of the track resulted in reclosure of the line in 1978. [Hurricane Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Allen "Hurricane Allen") in 1980 damaged much of the JRC railway system, and totally destroyed a section of the Port Antonio line running along the coast between [Buff Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buff_Bay "Buff Bay") and Orange Bay.

In October 1992 public railway transport services ceased operating on Jamaica,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3) although four of the private industrial lines continue to operate today, in part using JRC lines.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-Britannia-15) Of the total of 272 kilometres (169 mi) standard gauge at the time on the island, 207 kilometres (129 mi) of common carrier service belonging to JRC are no longer operational, leaving 65 kilometres (40 mi) in private hands.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JNHT2-16)

The Jamaican Railway Corporation still exists today (see below under "Revival"). It is responsible for management of the JRC interests and property, and maintaining its locomotives but not the rolling stock.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-17)

In November 1990 JRC signed a 30-year Track User Agreement with Alcan Jamaica, which was renegotiated with the successor [Windalco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusal "Rusal") in December 2001.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-18)

The company makes J$40 million per year through track user fees for the hauling of alumina and bauxite, and the residual from the rental of real estate and its three operable locomotives. The company has a staff of 76, who fulfil contractual obligations to users of the company's facilities.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamObs1-19)

In 2002 Jamaican Government discussed resumption of national railway services, initially with [Canadian National Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_National_Railway "Canadian National Railway")[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-20) and then [Rail India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Railways "Indian Railways") [Technical and Economic Service (RITES)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RITES "RITES");[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamObs1-19) and now with the [China Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Railway "China Railway") after a deal was signed by the Prime Minister [P J Patterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_J_Patterson "P J Patterson") with Chinese vice-president [Zeng Qinghong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeng_Qinghong "Zeng Qinghong") in Jamaica in February 2005.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-21) During the 1990s, a plan was considered which would see commuter services between Kingston and [Spanish Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Town "Spanish Town"), later extended to [Linstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linstead "Linstead"). It was proposed to cost [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_dollar "US dollar")8 million and be running by January 2001, with the government holding 40% of a public-private venture.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamGlen2-22)

Passenger service returned to Jamaica for the first time since February 1992 on 16 April 2011, when an inaugural train operated from [May Pen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Pen "May Pen") to [Linstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linstead "Linstead").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-25may-23) There was also talk of establishing a [tourist route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_railway "Heritage railway") on Jamalco's line between Rocky Point and Breadnut,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-24) but all passenger services were stopped again in August 2012.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JG20120814-4)

In 2022, the rail status shifted again, as a passenger service began transporting students from Old Harbour and Linstead to Spanish Town.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-25)

Records of the railway being used for mail service exist as far back as 1873 (when the postmaster terminated the railway's mail contract). [\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-Moh-26)

From 1 September 1913 sorting carriages were added to trains on the main routes: Kingston to Port Antonio and Kingston to Montego Bay.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-RSP-27) These carriages were fitted with posting boxes.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-RSP-27)

The travelling post office service resumed on 28 March 1927.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TPO-28) Its last run was on 14 May 1966.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-29) An official note c.1954 stated that "passenger trains between Kingston and Montego Bay (TPO 1) and Kingston and Port Antonio (TPO 2) are each equipped with a post office with a postman in charge. There is a letter-box at each station which the train postman clears en route."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TPO-28)

The railway architecture, developed and seen through the stations which were built between 1845 and 1896, is a reflection of classical [Jamaican Georgian architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Georgian_architecture "Jamaican Georgian architecture").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JNHT1-1) Although under the care and maintenance of the JRC, those that are not used for commercial purposes and rented out to traders are presently in a state of disrepair.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamObs1-19)

The Jamaica Railways have two serious accidents:

*   30 July 1938 - a passenger train was heading from Kingston to Montego Bay. The engine jumped the rails at [Balaclava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaclava,_Jamaica "Balaclava, Jamaica") and embedded itself into the mountainside, followed by coaches which were forced on from the rear. 32 people died and over 70 were injured.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamGlen2-22)
*   1 September 1957 - a diesel-hauled train of 12 wooden carriages left Kingston for Montego Bay. The outbound journey had 900 passengers on board, correlating with the design limit of 80 passengers per carriage. However, the return journey had 1,600 passengers loaded at 130-150 persons per carriage including hundreds of members of the Holy Name Society of St. Anne's Roman Catholic Church, 'close to a hundred known criminals' including [pickpockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickpocketing "Pickpocketing"), and their targets the tourists who made up over 1,000 of the total passenger loading. At 23:30 near Kendal, [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_Jamaica "Manchester, Jamaica") three shrill whistle blasts signalled that the driver had lost control of the train, and it derailed minutes later at speed.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamGlen2-22) 200 people lost their lives, and 700 sustained injuries in the worst transport disaster in Jamaica's history, and the second worst rail disaster in the world at that time. The cause of the accident was determined to be the closure of an angled wheel (brake) cock, with survivors suggesting that the pickpockets had tampered with the brakes while riding on the carriage platforms.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JamGlen2-22) Confidence in the rail service was shaken and much looting and robbing of the dead and injured occurred. The ensuing investigation found deficiencies in the Jamaica Railway Corporation, which was resultantly given its independence in 1960.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-JTH-3)

*   14 January 1907 - Kingston experienced [a great earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1907_Kingston_earthquake "1907 Kingston earthquake") which demolished many railway buildings and killed or injured officials, officers and employees.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TPO-28)
*   18 May 1909 - Number 2 railway pier in Kingston destroyed by fire.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-TPO-28)
*   1951 - [Hurricane Charlie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Charlie_/(1951/) "Hurricane Charlie (1951)") caused extensive damage to railway infrastructure.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-Moh-26)
*   1988 - [Hurricane Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Gilbert "Hurricane Gilbert") caused extensive damage to railway infrastructure.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Jamaica#cite_note-Moh-26)

The Corporation has a General Manager, also known (in the 21st century) as the Chief Executive Officer.

[This website has been archived from TrainWeb.org/ontariorailways to TrainWeb.US/ontariorailways.](https://www.trainweb.us/)

* * *

_**Location:**_ The Kingston & Pembroke Railway is located in eastern Ontario, connecting the Lake Ontario port city of Kingston with Renfrew in the Ottawa Valley. The line was never constructed beyond Renfrew to Pembroke.

_**History:**_ The Kingston & Pembroke Railway (K&PR) was incorporated in April 1871 by a group of local Kingston businessmen for the purpose of constructing a rail line north to a point in the Ottawa Valley at or near Pembroke. Additional powers were also granted at that time for branch lines extending east into Quebec. The project was one of many that were floating around at the time, the intent being to secure for the community of Kingston a share in the natural resources (logging and mining) and potential markets available to the north. Financing for the project was to be taken care of by counties and communities affected, in addition to traditional government aid. It was anticipated that the terminus for the railway would be on the Kingston waterfront where yards, docks, a roundhouse and warehouse facilities would be constructed.

Surveying of the line began in 1872 with construction commencing soon after from Kingston. Progress was initially slow, however, given the rough terrain to be found to the north of the city, and the continual shortage of capital. In June 1875, the company was reorganized and the first portion of track opened 29 miles north to a place known as Iron Junction. As well, a small branch line was built east from the mainline at Godfrey into a mine at Glendower. By May 1876, the project had reached Sharbot Lake 47 miles north of Kingston while, in the fall of 1878, the railway was completed to Mississippi. In Kingston via the Grand Trunk Railway (GTR), connections were made with American boat lines, allowing for the transfer of passengers and material across to Cape Vincent, New York.

With the completion of the Canada Central Railway north along the Ottawa River Valley to Mattawa in 1876, the necessity to close the gap at Pembroke became less critical. Even at that time, there was no need for the duplication of lines in the area. Accordingly, the K&PR was granted powers to make connections with the Canada Central at any point before Pembroke. In the interim, work continued on the rail line, opening to Lavant in 1881, Clyde Forks in 1882, and Barryvale in 1883. As well, the Glendower branch was extended several miles east to Zaneville. In 1884, the mainline was open to Calabogie. It was in this area that the K&PR was forced to spend substantial amounts of money on track construction, having to deal with major trestle, fill and rock cut works. From Calabogie, there remained only fifteen more miles to Renfrew where connections could be made with the CPR. The gap was finally joined by the end of that year. This was as close, however, as the line would get to its namesake community, Pembroke.

The next major construction initiative for the company was extending its tracks south to the Kingston waterfront in 1886, portions of the right-of-way being shared with the GTR. Here, the company built a new station and other terminal buildings. Other changes to the operation of the line included the obtainment of running rights by the Napanee, Tamworth & Quebec Railway from Harrowsmith south to Kingston in 1889, a situation that continued until 1925 when Canadian National chose to suspend further use. The volume of Ottawa Valley traffic originally anticipated by the railway never really materialized for the K&PR, forcing the company to rely primarily on local traffic. This became increasingly difficult given the sparse population of the lands the railway served, in addition to competition from motor vehicles. The main sources of revenue, however, tended to be derived from lumber and some iron and ore traffic. In 1894, the company fell into receivership, a situation that existed until 1899. By this time, the CPR had expressed interest in purchasing the company, hoping to keep it out of the hands of the GTR. Operation of the line was assumed in November 1901 with a 999 year lease being entered into in 1912. Over time, the infrastructure of the company was upgraded and the road bed rebuilt. Eventually, though, the K&PR became just another spoke in the nation wide CPR transportation system.

_**Approximate Milage:**_ 103 miles.

_**Current Status:**_ Under the Canadian Pacific, the line became known as the Kingston Subdivision. The entire line has been abandoned in the following manner: Snow Road to Calabogie in January 1962, Tichborne to Sharbot Lake in February 1964, Sharbot Lake to Snow Road in September 1966, Calabogie to Renfrew Junction in February 1977, and from Kingston to Tichborne in 1986.

_**Principle Stations:**_ Kingston, Sharbot Lake, Calabogie and Renfrew.

_**Remaining Stations:**_ There are nine stations remaining from the Kingston & Pembroke Railway. They are as follows:  
1\. Barryvale: Moved to property on Highway 511 as a summer residence.  
2\. Calabogie: Moved to property on Highway 511 as an antique store, unconfirmed.  
3\. Clarendon Station: In situ within hamlet off Highway 509 as a private residence.  
4\. Clyde Forks: Moved to property nearby as a boat house, unconfirmed.  
5\. Kingston: In situ at 209 Ontario Street as Chamber of Commerce offices and tourist info centre.

The **Kingston Subdivision**, often called the **Kingston Sub**, is a very important [railway line](https://kids.kiddle.co/Railway_track "Railway track") in Canada. It connects two of Canada's biggest cities, [Toronto](https://kids.kiddle.co/Toronto "Toronto") and [Montreal](https://kids.kiddle.co/Montreal "Montreal"). This railway line is used by many trains, especially those belonging to the [Canadian National Railway](https://kids.kiddle.co/Canadian_National_Railway "Canadian National Railway") (CN). It carries most of CN's freight (cargo) traffic between these two major cities.

This railway line was first built by the Grand Trunk Railway. It was their main route between Toronto and Montreal. Most of the Kingston Sub runs very close to the northern shore of [Lake Ontario](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lake_Ontario "Lake Ontario") and the [Saint Lawrence River](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Lawrence_River "St. Lawrence River").

[![Image 12: CN on the Kingston Subdivision in October 1981 02 (24338635946)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/2/28/CN_on_the_Kingston_Subdivision_in_October_1981_02_%2824338635946%29.jpg/300px-CN_on_the_Kingston_Subdivision_in_October_1981_02_%2824338635946%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:CN_on_the_Kingston_Subdivision_in_October_1981_02_/(24338635946/).jpg)

A CN train on the Kingston Subdivision in October 1981.

Contents
--------

*   [How the Kingston Sub Works](https://kids.kiddle.co/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#How_the_Kingston_Sub_Works)
    *   [Train Speeds and Control](https://kids.kiddle.co/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#Train_Speeds_and_Control)
    *   [Connecting Lines and Ownership](https://kids.kiddle.co/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#Connecting_Lines_and_Ownership)
*   [Stations Along the Line](https://kids.kiddle.co/CN_Kingston_Subdivision#Stations_Along_the_Line)

How the Kingston Sub Works
--------------------------

The Kingston Sub has two main tracks. Along these tracks, there are more than 50 special sections called crossover tracks. These crossovers let trains switch from one track to another very quickly.

### Train Speeds and Control

Trains carrying large shipping containers can change tracks at speeds up to 45 miles per hour. Passenger trains, like those from Via Rail, can switch tracks at 60 miles per hour, and even 90 miles per hour in some areas.

The entire railway line is controlled by a system called CTC. This system uses signals to tell trains when they can move and where they can go. Since 1995, train conductors on the Kingston Sub don't need to fill out special forms to get permission to move. The CTC signals give them all the necessary instructions. This is how most main railway lines work for CN.

### Connecting Lines and Ownership

Just east of Newcastle, near Toronto, another major railway line joins the Kingston Sub. This is the CP Belleville Subdivision, which belongs to the [Canadian Pacific Railway](https://kids.kiddle.co/Canadian_Pacific_Railway "Canadian Pacific Railway"). Both lines run side-by-side until east of [Belleville](https://kids.kiddle.co/Belleville,_Ontario "Belleville, Ontario"). There, the Belleville Sub turns north towards Smiths Falls.

Not all parts of the Kingston Sub are still owned by CN. For example, CN's main freight trains in the Toronto area now use a different route, the York Sub, which goes north of the city. The section of the Kingston Sub between Pickering Junction and Union Station in downtown Toronto was sold to Metrolinx. Metrolinx uses this part for their GO Transit service, which is part of their Lakeshore East line.

Stations Along the Line
-----------------------

The original Grand Trunk Railway line, built in the 1850s, had 34 stations. Many of these old stations are no longer used or have been taken down. For example, the Lansdowne station was removed after CN stopped service there in 1966. An Iroquois station was also taken down by CN in 2002.

Here are some of the stations currently on the main railway line between Toronto and Montreal:

*   Union Station (Toronto)
*   GO Transit stations (no VIA Rail service) in Toronto: Danforth, Scarborough, Eglinton
*   Guildwood
*   Commuter stations for GO Transit (no VIA Rail service) in: Rouge Hill/Pickering, Ajax, and Whitby
*   Oshawa GO Station
*   Port Hope railway station
*   Cobourg railway station
*   Brighton (not in use, now part of the [Memory Junction railway museum](https://kids.kiddle.co/Memory_Junction_Railway_Museum "Memory Junction Railway Museum"))
*   Trenton Junction railway station
*   [Belleville station (Ontario)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Belleville_station_/(Ontario/) "Belleville station (Ontario)")
*   Napanee railway station
*   Ernestown (not in use)
*   Kingston railway station (Ontario)
*   Kingston Outer Station (abandoned and in ruins)
*   Gananoque railway station
*   Brockville railway station
*   Prescott (not in use, now a historical society)
*   Near Morrisburg, two old stations from The Lost Villages were moved but not put back into service. New stations were built in Morrisburg and Long Sault in the 1950s, but trains no longer stop there.
*   Cornwall railway station
*   Dorval railway station (Via)
*   The line used to end at Bonaventure Station in Montreal. Now, it ends at Montreal Central Station.

Railway Stations ================ Historical Significance ----------------------- ![Image 2: Railway Stations](http://www.jnht.com/_images/thumb_railway_stations.jpg) The Jamaica Railway, constructed in 1845, was the first line opened to traffic outside Europe and North America. The rail service was established in the United Kingdom in 1825, the United States in 1830 and Canada in 1836. Not only did the Jamaica Railway have the distinction of being constructed so soon after the first public railway in Britain, but also, it was the first constructed in the British colonies. In 1843, a proposal to construct the railway line was made by William Smith and his brother David Smith to the House of Assembly in Jamaica. The plan to construct the double track line between Kingston and Spanish Town was favourably received by the Assembly and in the same year the Jamaica Railway Company was incorporated under the 7th Victoria cap. 25. Inherent Features ----------------- The railway stations constructed between 1845 and 1896 demonstrate the application of the Jamaica/Georgian style of architecture. It should be emphasized that although most of the stations were constructed as part of a major line extension, their individual form and features show great variety. Today, most of the stations are in a state of disrepair. Some are now used as bars, grocery shops or residences. Many stations have alterations made to their original form, nevertheless the original design features remain intact. * [Anchovy Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_anchovy_railway_station.php) \- is a two storey Jamaica/Georgian timber structure. * [Appleton Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_appleton_railway_station.php) \- is a two storey Jamaica/Georgian timber structure. * [Balaclava Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_balaclava_railway_station.php) - is a Jamaica/Georgian two storey building constructed of timber throughout. * [Bog Walk Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_Bog_walk_railway_station.php) - consists of a simple two-storey timber structure. * [Cambridge Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_cambridge_railway_station.php) - is a two-storey timber, unique Jamaica/Georgian style building. * [Catadupa Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_catadupa_railway_station.php) - is a two-storey Jamaica/Georgian timber structure. * [Four Paths Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_four_paths_railway_station.php) - is a two-storey concrete building. * [Greenvale Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_greenvale_railway_station.php) - is a two-storey Jamaica/Georgian timber structure. * [Kingston Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_kingston_railway_station.php) - was built along the Jamaica/Georgian lines of architecture. * [Linstead Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_linstead_railway_station.php) - boasts a very simple Jamaica/Georgian style of architecture. * [Montego Bay Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_montego_bay_railway_station.php) - is a simple timber building. * [Montpelier Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_montpelier_railway_station.php) - is a uniquely two-storey designed Jamaica/Georgian style of architecture. * [Old Harbour Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_old_harbour_railway_station.php) - is a two-storey Jamaica/Georgian structure. * [Orange Bay Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_orange_bay_railway_station.php) - demonstrates Jamaica/Georgian features. * [Riversdale Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_riversdale_railway_station.php) - is a two storey Jamaica/Georgian timber building. * [Spanish Town Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_spanish_town_railway_station.php) - is a Jamaica/Georgian style brick building set on a stone base. * [Suttons Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_suttons_railway_station.php) - is a Jamaica/Georgian timber house set on a stone base. * [Williamsfield Railway Station](http://www.jnht.com/site_williamsfield_railway_station.php) - has elements of the Jamaica/Georgian architectural style.

Jamaica embarks on a new rail journey
=====================================

*   By [RAIL magazine](https://www.railmagazine.com/author/rail-magazine)
*   |
*   19 May 2023
*   News

[](https://www.railmagazine.com/news/network/2023/05/17/uk-aids-jamaican-reopening#)

![Image 6](https://railm.blob.core.windows.net/website/1/root/screen-shot-2023-05-17-at-113616_w960.png)

Think of Jamaica, and railways probably aren’t the first thing that springs to mind. Tourism probably tops the list, and an initiative is under way - the Jamaica Community Rail Project (JCRP) - to transform a derelict station and rail line into a tourist attraction.

Construction work on the Caribbean island’s first railway infrastructure began just 20 years after that for the Stockton and Darlington Railway, with services on the Western Jamaica Connecting Railway beginning in 1845.

Initially, the line ran from Kingston to Spanish Town and was just 14½ miles long. In 1879, the privately owned railway was sold to the government, which funded the line’s extension to several other towns, before selling it on to the West Indian Railway Improvement Company.

The lines and services continued to be gradually extended, albeit in a limited way, linking more towns. But there was relatively little change over the following decades, other than the arrival of diesel trains in 1938.

12.content:
After looking at the [Kingston Railway Station](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/2021/05/02/jamaicas-railway-stations-kingston/) in my last post, it made sense to continue the story by just following the rail lines that departed from it. Today I will be looking at what’s left of the first rail line established in Jamaica, the 14.5 mile Kingston to Spanish Town railway.

Now before I get into this, let me cover some basic definitions that I forgot to mention last time, but will certainly pop up in this article:

*   **Halt:** Essentially a mini railway station. These were usually just elevated platforms with no staff that would just be somewhere passengers could hop on or hop off the train in-between Railway Stations. Unlike Railway Stations, which a train would always stop at, a train would only stop at a Halt at the request of a passenger.
*   **Level Crossing**: This is the point where a road and a railway cross paths. More commonly known as Railway Crossings
*   **Terminus**: This was the last Railway Station on the line. The place where all rail lines terminated. Kingston Railway Station was the terminus for the entire Jamaica Railway Corporation, something I forgot to mention in my last post.

With that out of the way, let’s get back to the Kingston to Spanish Town line.

Leaving the Kingston Railway Station
------------------------------------

So, imagine this, you’re a mid 19th century Spanish Town resident who has been living there all your life. You decide to take a trip to Kingston to see what all the drama is about. By now, a lot of companies and government facilities have begun to move to Kingston, and you’re considering to jump on the hype as well. After spending a weekend there, you realize that dusty ass Kingston with it’s noise, cholera and general Port Royal 2.0 vibe isn’t working for you. So back home to the clean air of Spanish Town it is. Now of course you can’t just drive back to Spanish Town because the car is still half a century away from being invented, so you hop on the Spanish Town bound train at the Kingston Railway Station, the quickest way there for now. Up until probably around the early 20th century, the Kingston Railway station was the western boundary for Kingston and as such the rail lines were mostly passing through trees and farm land before then. So as a mid 19th century traveler, it’s pretty uneventful outside of the one stop in Gregory Park (and possibly Grange Lane?). Scenic, yes, but nothing out of the ordinary for the time. So what does this mostly unremarkable journey look like today?

*   ![Image 1](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/kingston-lines-1.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Map of the Kingston segment of the Railway (yes, I used the difficult to read, but stylish font, Raleway)
    

Today, Industrial Terrace demarks the end of the property of the Kingston Railway Station. While driving on it recently, I was trying to see if I could try to find the old locomotive shed which was supposed to be around here, but the area was so overgrown, searching would have been futile (and dangerous). I do recall there being a level crossing on Industrial Terrace some 8 years ago, but it appears to have been paved over some time around the period of the construction of the 3 Miles overpass.

From there, the railway continues north west, parallel to Spanish Town Road. While it would have been great to follow the track, I didn’t want to venture into May Pen Cemetery or Greenwich Town (which was under a ZOSO) unnecessarily just to see some metal strips in the ground. Before I pick up back the railway at Marcus Garvey Drive, somethings to mention. According to Wikipedia\*, there was a Halt in Greenwich Town at some point in time, but, I was unable to confirm it (which I would have wanted to do, especially since [my reference](https://books.google.com.jm/books/about/The_Railways_of_Jamaica.html?id=zpxsjwEACAAJ&redir_esc=y) makes no mention of it). There is also a locomotive in neighboring [Trench Town](https://twitter.com/dempsterchung/status/1233906049477947397/photo/1) that I wanted to get a look at, but I mistakenly thought it was in Greenwich Town. I’ll save that for another time.

Leaving Greenwich Town, the railway makes it’s way across Marcus Drive, right at Tinson Pen Aerodrome. I do remember seeing the level crossing in the early 2000’s, in fact, cars slowing to cross the rails created a bottleneck for those making their way to and from 3 Miles. This justified it’s removal (and served to justify the removal of other level crossings) some time during the construction of the Portmore Causeway Toll Road in 2006. Much of the railway after this level crossing was also removed later on in 2018 to allow for a [2 lane bypass of 3 Miles](https://jamaica-gleaner.com/article/lead-stories/20180918/new-three-miles-bypass-bring-relief-motorists). The bypass was needed as the overpass construction at 3 Miles (one of Kingston’s busiest intersections) created major congestion, necessitating the use of alternative routes. Again, Wikipedia\* states that there was a Halt located somewhere around here, but I couldn’t find no evidence of it. Then again, I’m not getting paid to do this so my search really and truly consisted of just driving past twice.

*   ![Image 2](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_092343779-2.jpg?w=1024)
    
    On the 3 Mile Bypass, which displaced rails from Marcus Garvey Drive to Chesterfield Ave
    
*   ![Image 3](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_092512314-2-1.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Where the 3 Miles Bypass ends and the rails re-emerge
    

As the 3 Miles Bypass comes to an end at Chesterfield Drive, the railway emerges again in Seaview Gardens. Again, Wikipedia\* states that there was a Halt here (but the Almighty Reference doesn’t) There is space here to suggest that there was though.

*   ![Image 4](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_092702152_hdr-2.jpg?w=968)
    
    Open lot in Seaview Gardens with rails still visible
    
*   ![Image 5](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_092958759_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Bridge crossing the Sandy Gully, leaving Seaview Gardens and into Portmore. Bridge in the background carries sewage from Kingston to the Soapberry Treatment Plant
    

Leaving Seaview Gardens, the Railway crosses the Sandy Gully into St. Catherine, passing the Riverton Dump and then the Soapberry Wastewater Treatment Plant. Somewhere around this region, a tramline met up with the railway which travelled north into the canefields of Caymanas, crossing Mandela Highway near the entry to the PJ Patterson Highway (which some of you may remember). This tram line, long disused, was removed in [2018 during the widening of Mandela Highway](https://jis.gov.jm/mandela-highway-upgrading-project-89-per-cent-complete/). It would have been nice to venture into Soapberry to look for remnants of the rails, but a) it’s private property that’s 105% dirt roads, b) the almighty source says that both rails were long removed and c) it’s a sewage plant so it’s gonna smell like shit (among other things)

*   ![Image 6](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_091006063-2.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Railway Bridge visible from Dyke Road. Here the rail crosses the Rio Cobre on it’s way from Soapberry into Portmore.
    

\*As we know, using Wikipedia as a reference is an art rather than a science. [The reference they use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_to_Montego_Bay_railway) in identifying Halts is an [archived Annual Transport Statistics Report](https://web.archive.org/web/20130315174612/http://www.mtw.gov.jm/general_information/reports/TransportStatisticsReport2003_2004.pdf) from the Ministry of Transport and Works dated July 2005. The report (as far as I can see) only makes mention of one Halt in Kingston and St. Andrew, the Marcus Garvey Drive Halt. The other reference Wikipedia uses are 1:50,000 maps of Jamaica from the UK Directorate of Overseas Surveys. It really doesn’t make sense I chase that seeing as they were dissolved in 2001. By the way, the ‘Almighty Reference’ I constantly refer to is the book, ‘The Railways of Jamaica” by Jim Horsford

Portmore
--------

*   ![Image 7](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/portmore-map-1.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Map of the Portmore leg of the Railway. Yes I switched from Wikimapia to Google Maps because Wikimapia had Grange Lane disappearing for some strange reason.
    

The first stop is the Gregory Park Railway Station, which sadly burnt down not too long after the passenger railway service ended in 1992. Like the St. Margaret’s Bay, Albany, Maggoty, Kendal, and as of last month, Balaclava Railway Stations they were destroyed by fire no thanks in part to their predominant timber construction. Timber was the choice material of construction outside of the major towns, primarily due to availability. And before you bark at me saying “of course Portmore is major town” keep in mind the Railway was built when Portmore was all banana fields. Finding persons and material to work with timber would have been much easier than if it was done via brick. At most, you had a brick ground floor, with timber construction above. The railway and some of the platform is mostly intact. Railway Crossing signals still stand near the level crossing, which has not been paved over (yet). The lands of the Gregory Park Railway Station is almost fully overgrown with trees growing in the middle of the platform and railway.

*   ![Image 8](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_085414054_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Gregory Park Railway Station with only it’s Brick Platform remaining
    

*   ![Image 9](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_085246098.jpg?w=1024)
    
*   ![Image 10](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_085259717_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
*   ![Image 11](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_085426655.jpg?w=768)
    

The railway continues west, cutting between Gregory Park and Cedar Grove, to then cross Municipal Boulevard. This level crossing was paved over sometime in the 2010s. I’m not sure exactly when, but I do remember driving across it one day, and it disappearing under asphalt not too long after. The railway then runs between Grange Lane and the PJ Patterson Highway. There was a level crossing at Grange Lane, but that has long since been paved over. Somewhere near here is the Grange Lane Railway Station. What’s odd is that for the longest while I assumed the Grange Lane stop was just a Halt. It didn’t help that I could not find historical pictures of it unlike other Railway Stations. So as with previous Halts, I just did my customary 2 drive-bys, gave up, and called it a day. It’s not until now when I’m doing my final edits to this article that I realize that the Almighty Reference (and Wikipedia) calls it a Railway Station, not a Halt, meaning there was/is a building around here somewhere. Now because of this oversight, I gotta take another look through Grange Lane to find it sometime in the future. More than likely I’ll add it as a bonus post, because I am surely gonna miss a lot of things trying to cover the Railway Stations.

After Grange Lane, the line then continues through Lakes Pen and across the Spanish Town Bypass into Spanish Town (again the level crossing here is paved over)

Spanish Town Railway Station
----------------------------

*   ![Image 12](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075144907.jpg?w=1024)
    

The Spanish Town Railway Station, or should I say, the Spanish Town City Church, is a mostly brick and concrete structure and appears to be in fairly good condition, on the outside at least. As with most of these structures, the brick would have been the original building, with the concrete section added on around the 20th century. Concrete became the material of choice for construction after the 1907 Earthquake highlighted just how susceptible brick and timber can be.

*   ![Image 13](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075026031_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Entry to the Spanish Town City Church
    
*   ![Image 14](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075056217_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Concrete addition extended from the original brick structure. The demarcation is clear by the change in roof profile.
    
*   ![Image 15](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075109599.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Railway looking towards the junction. Remnants of a train scale visible on the right
    
*   ![Image 16](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075127951.jpg?w=1024)
    
*   ![Image 17](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075217125_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    

Is the building still in use? It looks so. I visited on a Saturday though so I cannot be sure. Making another visit on Sunday could be for naught considering church services are restricted as part of our pandemic guidelines. Now this is an assumption so don’t quote me in your research papers, but it appears that the Church occupies the space that would be used by passengers awaiting the train. Station offices and ticket booths look as though they are being used by other entities, such as the Jamaica Community Cadet Corps.

*   ![Image 18](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/spanish-town.jpg?w=1024)
    
    Map of Spanish Town Railway Station and Junction. The lines departing from the Junction towards Angels and Old Harbour are clearly visible due to being in constant use. Meanwhile, lines leading to and from the Railway Station are barely visible due to overgrowth
    

Outside of multiple lines and a train scale, the only other thing that stood out from a standard Railway Station was that Spanish Town was one of the few stations that had a junction. Trains could either travel west on to the Montego Bay Line or continue north on to the Port Antonio Line. There also appeared to be a line coming from March Pen Road into the Railway Station (separate from the line coming from Kingston). No reference I have can identify it’s use or destination. The Railway station also housed some locomotives and passenger train cars in it’s yard. Some of the passenger cars appear to be the ones used during the [2011 resumption of the Linstead to Spanish Town railway](http://radiojamaicanewsonline.com/local/linstead-spanish-town-rail-service-rolling), evidenced by their “How did you know I was Jamaican?” liveries. The Locomotives themselves appear to be the standard ALCO diesel electric locomotives in use from the 40s till now. Also present was a rail inspection car.

*   ![Image 19](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075511174.jpg?w=1024)
    
    L-R ALCO Locomotive behind a train of unrestored passenger cars. Inspection car can be seen in pink in the foreground
    
*   ![Image 20](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_075820110_hdr-1.jpg?w=1024)
    
    ALCO Locomotive with restored passenger train in the background.
    

Not too long after I took the above images I had to run out of there because I heard a train passing by the Spanish Town Junction and I wanted to catch a sight of it. I do want to make a return visit here to capture things I may have certainly missed, but until then, let’s continue past the Spanish Town Junction, north to the final stop of the original line, the Angels’ Halt. Before we get there, the references do make mention of a Halt at St. John’s Road, but I didn’t even drive past this time to check for it (I’m almost considering giving up looking for them altogether). Just before Angels, the railway crosses the Spanish Town Bypass one last time, which thankfully enabled me to [capture video of a train making it’s way past.](https://twitter.com/crossdrilled/status/1396227628730834945/video/1)

*   ![Image 21](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/spain-map-01.jpg?w=856)
    
    Map Showing the Spanish Town Rail Network
    

Angels’ Halt
------------

*   ![Image 22](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_081141482_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    
*   ![Image 23](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/img_20210522_081209449_hdr.jpg?w=1024)
    

Finally we come to the end of the original line, the Angels’ Halt. Composing of just a concrete platform, exciting right? This Halt is what I expect to see whenever I do my 1-2 drive-by, but sometimes, I feel like most Halts did not even have these. Despite being the end of the original line, there appears to be no turntables or additional lines, which leads me to believe that the train would have simply reversed from here back to Spanish Town on it’s return leg.

What Next?
----------

In 1867, the railway was expanded from Spanish Town westwards to Old Harbour. In 1879, the Government of Jamaica purchased the Jamaica Railway Company and began plans for the expansion of the railway to better suit it’s people. By 1885, the Old Harbour line was extended to Porus. Simultaneously, the Angels line extended through the Bog Walk Gorge via several tunnels on its way to Ewarton. After this, a deteriorating economy halted any further expansion for awhile and the Government of Jamaica sold the Jamaica Railway Company back to private hands. My next articles will take a look at this second phase of the railway. This second phase will be the most interesting to look at as it is mostly composed of railways which are still in use.

Of all the lines in Jamaica, the Kingston to Spanish Town line does appear to be the one that could be the most practical for passenger use. The congestion on the Portmore Causeway and Mandela Highway shows that there is a need for relief that a railway could provide. The feasibility of reintroducing this however, [needs another article to get into.](https://crossdrilled.home.blog/2021/05/24/kington-to-spanish-town-line-part-2-is-renovation-feasible/)

[Auto](https://www.jamaicaobserver.com/category/auto/)

July 12, 2024

JRC looking to commence work facilitating rail service expansion
================================================================

**The** **Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC) is looking to commence work towards launching phase one of the tourist train service between Montpelier, St James, and Appleton Estate in St Elizabeth.**

This engagement will involve, among other things, track reconstruction, acquisition of trains and constructing necessary infrastructure along the route.

The JRC also plans to kick-start preparations for the launch of passenger and freight train services between Spanish Town and Kingston.

Additionally, the company will finalise the roll-out of commercial rail service from Bodles Junction to Linstead in St Catherine, specifically for transporting aggregates.

These activities form part of the JRC’s programmed continuation this year of strategies targeting the entity’s improved positioning to revitalise and expand rail service and optimise its financial performance.

Details of these and other engagements are contained in the Jamaica Public Bodies of Estimates and Expenditure for the Fiscal Year ending 2024/25.

The JRC is also expected to commence discussions with private investors to secure funding for building rail infrastructure, rehabilitating existing rolling stock, acquiring new trains and upgrading the entity’s Kingston workshop.

Meanwhile, the entity plans to continue the monetisation of real estate properties owned, to generate optimum returns on the portfolio.

The corporation is also looking to expand its leased lands and properties, while considering the implementation of a cashless rental collection system for tenants.

The JRC is a statutory body formed under the Jamaica Railway Corporation Act of 1960.

16.content:
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) investigated this occurrence for the purpose of advancing transportation safety. It is not the function of the Board to assign fault or determine civil or criminal liability. **This report is not created for use in the context of legal, disciplinary or other proceedings.** See [Ownership and use of content](http://www.bst-tsb.gc.ca/eng/avis-notices/avis-notices.html#copy). Masculine pronouns and position titles may be used to signify all genders to comply with the _Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board Act_ (S.C. 1989, c. 3).

On 13 April 2023 at about 1451 Eastern Daylight Time, Canadian National Railway Company mixed freight train M 37231-13 was proceeding eastward on the south track of the Kingston Subdivision at about 43.2 mph when it passed signal 694S displaying a Stop indication at Wesco (Mile 69.4). At the same time, VIA Rail Canada Inc. passenger train P 06721-13 was travelling at approximately 45 mph westward on the south track of the Kingston Subdivision, approaching Wesco, where it was lined to cross over to the north track. Both trains stopped about 1100 feet apart. There were no injuries to either crew or to the passengers.

On 13 April 2023, a Canadian National Railway Company (Canadian National or CN) train crew was ordered for 0815All times are Eastern Daylight Time. in BellevilleAll locations are in the province of Ontario, unless otherwise indicated. to operate mixed freight train M 37231-13 (CN 372) from Belleville to Montréal, Quebec, via the CN Kingston Subdivision. CN 372 consisted of 2 locomotives in a distributed power configuration, with 1 locomotive at the head end and 1 about mid-train; it was hauling 113 loaded cars and 23 empty cars. The train included 16 cars loaded with dangerous goods and 17 residue cars last containing dangerous goods. It measured 9937 feet and weighed 12 592 tons. The train crew consisted of a locomotive engineer (LE) and a conductor. Both crew members were qualified for their respective positions, met fitness and rest requirements, and were familiar with the territory on which they operated.

That same morning, a VIA Rail Canada Inc. (VIA) train crew was ordered for 1123 in Montréal to operate passenger train P 06721-13 (VIA 67) from Montréal to Toronto, travelling on the CN Kingston Subdivision. VIA 67 consisted of 1 locomotive and 4 coach cars with 167 passengers on board. It weighed 332 tons and measured 398 feet. The train operating crew consisted of 2 LEs. Both crew members were qualified for their respective positions, met fitness and rest requirements, and were familiar with the territory on which they operated.

### 1.1 The occurrence

> Under section 28 of the _Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board Act_, every on-board recording is privileged. However, the TSB may make use of any on-board recording where it is necessary in the interests of transportation safety. For this reason, while the Board may refer to an on-board recording where required to support a finding and identify a substantive safety deficiency, other parties may not access or use privileged on-board recordings.
> 
> The reason for protecting on-board recordings lies in the premise that these protections will respect the privacy of operating personnel whose words and actions are captured on the recording and will also help ensure that this essential material is available for the benefit of the TSB’s safety investigations.
> 
> This report references content from a locomotive voice and video recorder (LVVR), which is a form of on-board recording in the rail sector. For each of these references, the TSB is using the LVVR recording to substantiate some of its findings and to identify certain substantive safety deficiencies. In each case, the material has been carefully examined to ensure that the extracts used are necessary to identify causes or contributing factors of this accident or to identify safety deficiencies.

CN 372 departed Belleville at 0850. At about 1313, the train stopped due to an air hose separation, and temporary repairs were made to car HESX 52 (position 38). CN management made the decision that the car should be set off the train at the next suitable location (Regis, Mile 65.4). The crew then discussed the suitability of the set-off location for the train length and the set-off procedure.

At about 1410, CN 372 resumed its journey eastward on the south track of the Kingston Subdivision. The crew consulted with the rail traffic controller (RTC) via radio about the car set-off and, on several occasions, they spent time accessing information on their company-issued tablets to prepare for the set-off at Regis. During this time, they also evaluated the suitability of an alternate set-off location, Coteau, Mile 37.8, to accommodate the train length.

At about 1448, CN 372 approached signal 716S (Mile 71.6), which was displaying a Clear to Stop indication.A Clear to Stop indication is used to inform train crews to proceed, preparing to stop at the next signal. The crew members were discussing the upcoming car set-off on the radio with the RTC and did not identify the signal indication and/or communicate it to each other. When the train was approximately 2650 feet from signal 716S, the call with the RTC ended. The crew members were still in conversation as the head end of their train passed the signal at approximately 52 mph.

At about 1449, the RTC contacted the crew on CN 372 again to further discuss the upcoming car set-off. The conversation lasted about 50 seconds.

At about 1450, while travelling at 49 mph, CN 372 approached the next signal, signal 694S, at Wesco near Cornwall (Mile 68.0) (Figure 1). Approximately 1400 feet from the signal, the crew observed the signal and questioned whether it was a Stop signal.The last signal that the crew identified before missing signal 716S was signal 740S, which displayed a Clear indication permitting the train to proceed. The LE then made a minimum brake application. About 13 seconds later, the conductor identified and communicated the Stop signal and placed the train in emergency. The train went past the Stop signal at 43.2 mph. The conductor made an emergency broadcast over the radio to communicate the situation as required by the _Canadian Rail Operating Rules_ (CROR). At 1452:08, CN 372 came to a stop at approximately Mile 69.1, 1786 feet past the Stop signal.

**Figure 1.** Map of the occurrence location, with inset map showing the location of Cornwall, Ontario (Source of main map: Railway Association of Canada, with TSB annotations. Source of inset map: Google Earth, with TSB annotations)

The same day, VIA 67 had departed Montréal at 1323, travelling westward on the Kingston Subdivision. It received a Clear to Limited indicationA Clear to Limited indication allows a train to proceed; however, the train must approach the next signal at limited speed. Limited speed is defined as a speed not exceeding 45 mph. \[Canadian National Railway Company, _Canadian Rail Operating Rules_ (effective 28 October 2021), Rule 406: Clear to Limited, p. 78, and Definitions (Speeds), p. 15.\] at signal 667S on the south track. At about 1450, while travelling at 45 mph, VIA 67 approached Wesco, where it was to cross over to the north track. At about 1451, upon hearing the emergency radio broadcast from the crew of CN 372, the LE at the controls of VIA 67 brought his train to a controlled stop. VIA 67 came to rest with the head end at approximately Mile 68.9, 1100 feet east of the head end of CN 372 (Figure 2). There were no injuries to either crew or to the passengers.

**Figure 2.** Head end of train CN 372, as seen from the locomotive on train VIA 67, after both trains had stopped (Source: VIA Rail Canada Inc.)

Figure 3 shows the location of the relevant signals, and the relative position of the stopped trains in relation to these signals and to each other.

**Figure 3.** Schematic of the track near the occurrence location (Source: TSB)

At the time of the occurrence, the temperature was 27 °C and the sky was clear; visibility was good.

### 1.2 Subdivision and track information

The CN Kingston Subdivision consists of 2 to 4 main tracks that extend from Dorval East in Montréal (Mile 10.3) to Toronto (Mile 333.8).

The subdivision is a major high-speed rail traffic corridor in Canada. An average of 18 CN freight trains and 12 VIA passenger trains operate on the subdivision daily.

Train movements are governed by the centralized traffic control system (CTC) as authorized by the CROR and are dispatched by a CN RTC located in Edmonton, Alberta.

The track in the vicinity of the occurrence consists of 2 main tracks (north and south). It is designated as a Class 5 track according to the _Rules Respecting Track Safety_. The maximum authorized speed is 100 mph for passenger trains and 65 mph for freight trains; however, on the day of the occurrence, the following speed restrictions were in effect:

*   A slow track protection restricted passenger trains to a maximum of 80 mph and freight trains to a maximum of 60 mph at Mile 69.4 on the south track.Canadian National Railway Company, Tabular General Bulletin Order No. 4079 (13 April 2023).
*   A timetable speed restriction required that eastward freight trains handling 80 or more tons per operative brakesTons per operative brake is the total weight of the train (including locomotives) divided by the total number of operative brake control valves on the train. Depending on the infrastructure and operational constraints, railways may apply speed restrictions on certain areas when the tons per operative brake on a train reach a specified threshold (in this occurrence, greater than 80 tons per operative brake). not exceed 60 mph approaching signals 716S (south track) and 716N (north track) at Mile 71.6.Canadian National Railway Company, _Eastern Canada Region – Champlain Division TimeTable 86_ (effective 01 February 2023).,CN 372 had a ratio of 92.6 tons per operative brakes and was therefore required to comply with this speed restriction.

### 1.3 Recorded information

The lead locomotive on CN 372 was equipped with a locomotive event recorder and a forward-facing video camera. A review of the data from these devices shows the following:

*   At 1448:45, the lead locomotive, travelling at 52 mph, passed signal 716S (Clear to Stop) at Mile 71.6.
*   At 1449:23, the lead locomotive, travelling at 51.6 mph, passed Mile 71.0 (1.6 miles from the Stop signal at Wesco).
*   At 1450:34, the lead locomotive, travelling at 49 mph, passed Mile 70.0 (3199 feet from the Stop signal at Wesco).
*   At 1451:06, the LE initiated a minimum brake application.
*   At 1451:13, while the train was travelling at 46.5 mph with the dynamic brake in position 8, an emergency brake application was registered while the lead locomotive was at Mile 69.3 (467 feet before the Stop signal at Wesco).
*   At 1451:20, the lead locomotive, travelling at 43.2 mph, passed signal 694S (Stop signal) at Mile 69.4.
*   At 1452:08, the lead locomotive came to a stop at Mile 69.1 after travelling roughly 2300 feet with an emergency brake application.

While playing back the data from the forward-facing video camera, the TSB observed that a windshield wiper was obstructing the view from the camera (Figure 4). During daylight operations, the signal views from the camera are limited by the camera resolution, which results in a limited opportunity to identify the signal indication. In this occurrence, this did not impede the crew’s ability to positively identify the signal.

CN requires that crews ensure the view from forward-facing cameras remains unobstructed at all times.Canadian National Railway Company, _Locomotive Engineer Operating Manual_ (01 May 2016), section A1.18: Locomotive Camera – Unobstructed View, p. 6.

**Figure 4.** View from the forward-facing camera on train CN 372, showing that the view is obstructed by a windshield wiper (Source: Canadian National)

The TSB has encountered this situation in 3 other occurrences since 2023, on recordings provided by CN and other railways.

Finding: Other

A forward-facing video camera is a useful tool in an accident investigation; however, in this occurrence, the view from train CN 372’s locomotive camera was partially obstructed by a windshield wiper, resulting in a limited opportunity to identify the signal indication.

#### 1.3.1 Locomotive voice and video recorder on the lead locomotive of CN 372

As part of its investigation, the TSB requested locomotive voice and video recorder (LVVR) data from the lead locomotive on CN 372.

While reviewing the data from CN 372, the TSB observed that the first 35 minutes of the recording did not contain in-cab audio. Canadian regulations require that both the in-cab video and audio must be recorded on trains operating in Canada.“A company must ensure that an LVVR system \[…\] continuously records voice and video data from the time the controlling locomotive engine is turned on until is it turned off.” (Source: Transport Canada, _Locomotive Voice and Video Recorder Regulations_, SOR/2020-178 \[last amended 02 September 2022 \], Technical Requirements, subsection 5(b))

This is the 3rd occurrence investigated by the TSB in which in-cab voice recording was not available.
